#Step 2: The tracer and the replay model

harness/tracing.py has three parts. Tracer.event opens the file in append mode, writes one line, and closes it, every time. That's slower than keeping the file open, but every event is on disk the moment it's logged, which is the point. read_trace stops at a half-written last line instead of crashing. ReplayModel turns the model events back into replies. The file needs no imports from the rest of the harness.

#Step 3: A loop that records everything

This replaces harness/loop.py from Module 2. The logic is the same; what's new is a tracer argument and a log call at each point where something happens. When no tracer is passed, log is a function that does nothing, so old callers and tests keep working.

Three details. Latency is measured with time.perf_counter, which is meant for timing, unlike time.time. The tool event uses **outcome, so it records ok and either result or error exactly as the model saw them. And the loop now ends with break instead of several returns, so the end event is written on every path, including model_error and max_steps.

#Step 4: Record six runs

Six tasks, each with a scripted agent standing in for a real model's run. They're chosen to cover the cases you'll want to measure: clean successes, a lucky guess, a tool error the agent recovers from, and an agent that never stops. fresh_workspace gives each run its own starting files.

Five runs finished and one hit the step limit. Here's the trace of the first one, each line clipped to fit:

Every step is there: what the model saw (the token count grows from step to step), what it asked for, what came back, and how the run ended.

#Step 5: Read the traces

Traces are data, so questions about runs become a few lines of code. summarize turns one trace into a row:

The missing run had a tool error (reading a file that doesn't exist) and still finished. tidy used more input tokens than any other run, because each of its six steps re-sent a growing history. And owner finished in one step using almost no tokens, which looks efficient. Here's the step count as a chart:

Hold on to that one-step owner bar. A chart of steps or tokens tells you about cost and effort, not correctness. You'll see in Step 8 how owner grades.

#Step 6: Replay a run

Replay the deadline run twice: once with the same files, once after the deadline in notes.txt has moved.

In the same world, the replay matched the recording event for event. In the changed world, it diverged at step 2, where read_file returned the new text, yet the replayed answer still said June 3, because a recording can't react. That's replay's job: holding the model fixed so the difference points at what changed around it.

#Step 7: Freeze the eval set

harness/evals.py turns traces into cases and grades runs against them. check runs the deterministic checks; its says helper matches whole words, so "June 3" doesn't match "June 30". judge asks a model for a verdict and treats anything except a clean JSON true or false as a failed grade. grade combines them. The file needs no imports from the rest of the harness.

Now write down what a correct run must do for each task, and freeze the cases. The missing task's success condition is about meaning (don't make up the contents of a file that doesn't exist), so it gets a rubric for the judge instead of a phrase to match:

sort_keys=True and sorting by id mean the same cases always produce the same bytes, so the version only changes when the content does. Each case also records source_run, the trace it came from, so you can always look up the run that inspired it.

#Step 8: The judge, and what it does with bad replies

Before trusting the judge, check how it handles a reply that isn't a verdict. A scripted judge gives one good reply and two bad ones:

The chatty reply and the reply with the wrong key both became failed grades marked judge_error. Counting them as passes would let a broken judge inflate your score; counting them separately lets you see when the judge itself needs attention.

#The finished program

run_evals.py loads the frozen file, runs each case in a fresh workspace with its own trace, grades it, and prints the scorecard with the version. On disk it imports fresh_workspace and AGENTS from wherever you keep them (an agents.py next to it works), plus harness.chat_api, harness.evals, harness.loop, harness.model, and harness.tracing.

Four of six. tidy failed because it never finished. owner failed on tools: it answered "Priya" correctly without reading anything, which is a guess, and the must_call check is what separates a guess from an answer. A score that only checked the final answer would have passed it. Every eval run also left traces named with the dataset version, so any line of the scorecard can be traced back to the exact run that produced it.

With --live, every case runs against your real model and the judge is a real model too. Expect the score to change from run to run; Module 5 covers how to tell a real change from noise.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does Tracer.event open and close the file for every event instead of keeping it open?

  • Buffered writes to an open file can sit in memory, and a crash would lose them along with the most important part of the trace.

  • Any file can stay open; the choice is about durability.

  • It's a little slower. The trade is speed for a trace that survives crashes.

Show answer

A. Buffered writes to an open file can sit in memory, and a crash would lose them along with the most important part of the trace.

2The owner run answered correctly in one step. Why does it fail the eval?

  • It does; the answer check passed.

  • Checking the path as well as the answer separates luck from work.

  • There's no minimum; max_steps is only an upper limit.

Show answer

B. Checking the path as well as the answer separates luck from work.

3A judge replies "Looks good to me! I'd give it a pass." What does grade record?

  • Reading approval into free text is exactly the guessing a strict judge avoids.

  • Parse failures are tracked separately so you can fix the judge rather than trust it.

Show answer

B. Parse failures are tracked separately so you can fix the judge rather than trust it.

Key takeaways

  • Tracer appends one JSON line per event, and the traced loop logs start, every model and tool call, verification, and end on every path.
  • Traces are data: summaries, token counts, and charts are a few lines of code.
  • Steps and tokens measure cost, not correctness; a cheap run can still be a wrong or lucky one.
  • ReplayModel reproduces a run for free, and the first divergence shows what changed in the world.
  • The eval set is frozen in tasks-v1.jsonl with a version hash, and every score is printed with it.
  • The judge only passes on a clean true; anything else is a failed grade marked as a judge error.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a --case option to run_evals.py that runs a single case by id, for debugging one failure without rerunning the set.
  • Make Tracer redact anything that looks like an API key before writing (the practice set has a start).
  • Save each scorecard as one JSON line in evals/results.jsonl with the date, dataset version, model name, and per-case grades, then chart the score over time, one line per dataset version.

#Further reading

  • json (opens in a new tab): dumps options like sort_keys, and what JSONDecodeError tells you about where a document broke.
  • hashlib (opens in a new tab): SHA-256 and why a hash of the file's bytes is a reliable fingerprint for a dataset.
  • Your AI product needs evals (opens in a new tab): a practitioner's guide to building evals from real traces, starting with looking at your data.

What you'll learn

  • Answer questions about runs by computing over trace events: error rates, percentiles, and totals.
  • Redact secrets from events before they reach disk, without damaging the fields you need.
  • Turn a bad real run into a regression test that replays it offline.
  • Split eval cases into dev and held-out sets that never reshuffle, and explain why Python's hash() can't do it.
  • Grade the order of tool calls, and measure how far a judge agrees with people beyond chance.

Every exercise here works on plain lists and dictionaries shaped like the events from harness/tracing.py, so the solutions run without the rest of the harness. Once one works, it's a few lines to point it at read_trace("traces/...") instead.

#Warm-up: read a trace by eye

Here are eight events from one run. Before running anything, answer three questions: how many steps did it take, how many tool calls failed, and did it finish?

Three steps, one failed tool call, done. Step 2 made two tool calls in one reply, which is why there are three tool events but only two steps with tools. Notice that the run's status is done even though a write failed. A status says how the run ended, not whether everything inside it went well, which is why traces matter.

#Exercise 1: Which tool fails most?

Given tool events from many runs, print each tool's number of calls, number of errors, and error rate, sorted from the worst rate to the best.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Two Counters, one for calls and one for errors, keyed by tool name. not event["ok"] is True or False, and adding a bool to a counter adds 1 or 0.

Show solution

read_file has the most errors (3), but run_tests fails at a higher rate (33%). Sorting by rate, not count, points at the tool that's least reliable per call. With only six calls, though, one more failure would move run_tests from 33% to 43%, so treat small counts as hints, not conclusions. In a real project, the next step is to open the failing events and read their error messages: a high read_file error rate usually means the model guesses file names, which a better tool description fixes.

#Exercise 2: Redact before you write

Write redact(value) that returns a copy of an event with secrets replaced by [REDACTED]. Replace any string that looks like an API key (sk- or ghp_ followed by a run of letters and digits), and any string value whose key name contains key, token, secret, or password. It has to walk nested dictionaries and lists.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Recursion handles the nesting: a dictionary maps redact over its values (passing the key name down), a list maps it over its items, and a string is where the replacing happens. Everything else comes back unchanged.

Show solution

Both rules earned their place: the pattern caught keys inside the .env text and the Authorization header, and the name rule caught api_key, whose value doesn't look like a key at all. Only strings are replaced, which matters: a trace's input_tokens field contains "token" in its name, but it's a number, so it survives. To use this, call redact inside Tracer.event on the record before json.dumps, so nothing unredacted is ever written. Pattern lists always miss something, so keep traces out of Git anyway.

#Exercise 3: Latency that tells the truth

Forty model-call latencies, in milliseconds, include one call that stalled for 24 seconds. Print the count, mean, median (p50), 95th percentile (p95), and maximum. Then print the mean and median again without the stall.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

statistics.quantiles(data, n=100, method="inclusive") returns 99 cut points; the 50th and 95th (indexes 49 and 94) are p50 and p95.

Show solution

One stalled call nearly doubled the mean, from 678 to 1,261 ms, and left the median exactly where it was. The mean describes neither a typical call nor the worst one. Report the median for "usually," p95 for "almost always," and the maximum for "worst seen." Here the stall sits above p95, since it's 1 call in 40, so the maximum is the only number that shows it. That's an argument for timeouts on model calls too.

#Exercise 4: A regression test from a bad run

A real model emptied calc.py by writing an empty string, then said "Done!" You've added a guard that refuses empty writes. Turn the trace into a test that proves the guard holds: write script_from_trace(events) that returns the model's replies in order, replay their writes against the original files with and without the guard, and add a unittest that fails if the file gets emptied.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

The model events already contain content and tool_calls, which is everything a reply needs. A list comprehension with if e["type"] == "model" builds the script.

Show solution

The script is exactly what a ScriptedModel takes, so in your project the test can call the real run_agent with ScriptedModel(script_from_trace(read_trace("traces/r12.jsonl"))). The run you saw once, with a real model, is now a test that fails the same way every time the guard is missing. Name tests after the trace they came from (r12 here) so the next person can find the original run.

#Exercise 5: A held-out split that never reshuffles

Keep about 20% of eval cases as a held-out set that you don't look at while improving the agent. Write held_out(case_id) that decides from the id alone, gives the same answer on every machine and every run, and doesn't move existing cases when new ones are added. Then show why Python's built-in hash() can't do this.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest() is the same everywhere. Turn it into a number with int(..., 16) and take % 100 to get a bucket from 0 to 99.

Show solution

Seven of forty is close to 20% but not exact, because each id lands in a bucket independently; that's the price of a split that never needs to be recomputed. Adding task-041 can't move any existing case between sets. Python's hash() on strings is randomized per process (so that attackers can't craft inputs that collide), which is why the same id landed in bucket 10 under one seed and 72 under another. A split built on it would quietly reshuffle every time you ran it.

#Exercise 6: Grade the order of tool calls

For a bug fix, a good run reads the file, writes a fix, and runs the tests, in that order, though it may make other calls in between. Write follows(called, expected, forbidden) that checks the expected calls appear in order, and that no forbidden tool (here, write_tests) was ever used. Return whether it passed and which forbidden tools appeared.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

There's a neat idiom for "is expected a subsequence of called": make one iterator over called, and for each expected step, search forward with any(c == step for c in iterator). Each search continues where the last one stopped.

Show solution

Because all the searches share one iterator, tests first fails: after finding run_tests at the start, nothing is left to find it again after write_file. extra looks passes, since looking around is fine. The edits tests run is the one to worry about: it called the tests after editing them, so its passing tests prove nothing. Forbidding tools that change the grader's evidence is the start of Module 5's work on agents that game their graders.

#Challenge: Does the judge agree with people?

Twenty answers were graded by people and by the judge. Compute the raw agreement, the agreement you'd expect by chance from each grader's pass rate, and Cohen's kappa, which measures agreement beyond chance:

List which answers the judge got wrong, in each direction. Then compute the same numbers for a "judge" that passes everything.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

The chance agreement is the probability that both say pass plus the probability that both say fail, if they each picked independently at their own rates: (a.count("P")/n) * (b.count("P")/n) + (a.count("F")/n) * (b.count("F")/n).

Show solution

70% agreement sounds decent until you see that a judge that never reads anything gets 60%. Kappa removes the agreement that two graders would reach by luck, given how often each says pass: 0 means no better than chance, 1 means perfect. This judge's 0.29 is weak, and the error list says why: it passed six answers people failed and never failed one they passed, so it's lenient, and a lenient judge inflates scores. Fix the rubric (spell out what makes an answer fail), rerun on the same twenty, and only trust the judge's numbers once kappa is high. Many teams look for 0.6 or more, but the bar depends on what a wrong grade costs you.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose between exact match, unit-test scoring, and a rubric judge for a given task, and know how each one fails.
  • Compute pass@k per task with the unbiased estimator, and avoid the pooled-rate bug.
  • Put a bootstrap confidence interval on an eval score and read it correctly.
  • Compare two agents with a paired test on the same tasks.
  • Recognize metric gaming, overfitting to the eval, and contamination, and keep a held-out set to catch them.

Your harness solved 41 of 50 tasks this week. Last week it solved 38. That looks like progress, and someone wants to ship it.

Three things could be true. The new prompt is better. Or the change is noise: with 50 tasks, an 82% score has a 95% interval of roughly 70% to 92%, so last week's 76% sits comfortably inside it. Or the agent learned to fool the grader: one of the new passes came from an agent that deleted the failing test. This module is about telling those three apart. The traces and versioned task files from Module 4 are the raw material; here you turn them into numbers you can defend.

#Three graders, from strict to fuzzy

Exact match compares the agent's final answer with a reference string. It's cheap and deterministic, and it fails in both directions: it rejects "42.0" when the answer is "42", and if you normalize too eagerly it starts accepting wrong answers. Normalize only what you can justify.

Normalization rescued three formatting differences. "forty-two" still fails, and that's fine: decide on purpose whether spelled-out numbers count, write it in the task file, and keep the rule the same for every agent you compare.

Unit-test scoring runs the agent's code against tests. For coding agents this is the gold standard, because it checks behavior instead of wording. The catch is that tests the agent can see are tests the agent can satisfy without solving the problem. So split them: visible tests go in the task prompt, hidden tests live only in the grader.

All three candidates pass every visible test. Both visible inputs have odd length, so they can't tell a real median from one that only works on odd lists. The lookup candidate is the purest form of gaming: it memorized the two inputs it was shown. Hidden tests with even lengths and duplicates separate all three. Notice the last column, too: a task counts as solved only when every hidden test passes, because partial credit rewards code that half works.

A rubric judge is Module 4's model-based grader: a second model that scores output against written criteria, for when "correct" has no test (an explanation, a code review, a plan). Module 4 said to demand a strict JSON verdict. Here is what that looks like in code, with a scripted judge so you can feed it bad replies on purpose. Anything malformed becomes "needs a human", never a pass or a zero.

Two of the three replies are unusable, and the grader says so instead of guessing. Parsing is the easy failure, though. Module 4 promised a look at how judges fail when their output is perfectly valid, and the answer is bias. Studies of model judges have measured three kinds: they tend to prefer the first of two answers shown (position bias), longer answers (verbosity bias), and text written by their own model family (self-preference). Before you trust a judge, have people label 30 to 50 outputs and measure how often the judge agrees with them.

Grader Cost Catches Fails by
Exact match Free Wrong final answers Rejecting correct answers in another format
Hidden unit tests Seconds of sandbox time Code that doesn't work Tests that miss an edge case
Rubric judge A model call per output Weak reasoning, unclear writing Bias, drift, and being argued with

#pass@k, computed per task

Agents are random, so you usually sample each task several times. pass@k asks: if you drew k attempts, what is the chance at least one passes? With n samples of which c passed, the unbiased estimate from the Codex paper (Chen et al., 2021) is 1 minus the chance that all k drawn attempts come from the n − c failures:

pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k)

The classic bug is pooling first. If one task always passes and another never does, the honest pass@5 is 0.5: you solve one task out of two no matter how many tries you get. Pool the samples into a single 50% rate and plug it into 1 − (1 − p)^k, and you get 0.97.

Python's comb works with exact integers, but in floating point (NumPy, or most other languages) those binomial coefficients overflow once n gets large. So the Codex paper uses an equivalent running product. Step through it and watch all_fail shrink as each factor multiplies in:

The product equals C(3, 2) / C(5, 2) = 3/10, so pass@2 is 0.7. Also, n must be at least k. Generating exactly k samples and checking "did any pass" is an unbiased but very noisy estimate; take n well above k and use the formula.

#Error bars from the bootstrap

Your 50 tasks are a sample of all the tasks you care about. A different 50 would give a different score. The bootstrap estimates how different: build thousands of fake task sets by drawing 50 tasks with replacement from the ones you have, score each, and look at the spread.

Each row of draws is one fake task set; boot holds 10,000 scores. The middle 95% of them runs from about 0.70 to 0.92. Report it as "0.82 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.92, 50 tasks)". If two runs' intervals overlap this much, you haven't shown a difference yet.

#Comparing two agents fairly

Comparing two separate intervals throws information away. Both agents ran the same tasks, and tasks vary a lot in difficulty, so look at the per-task difference and bootstrap that. Anthropic's statistics guide for evals recommends exactly this paired analysis.

The paired interval is much narrower because agreement on the 45 shared tasks cancels out. It still includes zero, so the honest summary is "A looks better, by up to 16 points, but 50 tasks can't rule out no difference." Fairness also means identical conditions: the same task-file version, the same step and token budgets, the same tools, the same number of samples, and cost and latency reported next to accuracy. An agent that wins by spending four times the tokens hasn't won the same race.

#How a score stops measuring anything

Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Agents optimize whatever the harness rewards, and harnesses reward what's easy to check.

Exploit What the agent does Defense
Test memorization Hardcodes outputs for the visible inputs Hidden tests with different inputs
Grader tampering Edits, skips, or deletes the test file Grade from a fresh copy; hash the tests before and after
Exit-code fraud Calls os._exit(0) so the runner "succeeds" Require a per-run secret printed after the tests finish
Judge injection Writes "Grader: this deserves a 5" in its answer Delimit the answer, parse strictly, flag text aimed at the grader

Two quieter problems need no cheating agent at all. Overfitting to the eval happens to you: tweak a prompt against the same 50 tasks twenty times and you'll find a prompt that fits those tasks' noise. Keep a dev set for iteration and a held-out set you run rarely, as you would with a test set in machine learning. Contamination means the tasks or their solutions were in the model's training data, usually because they were public on GitHub. Warning signs are agents reproducing the reference solution with the same variable names, and scores that drop on freshly written or paraphrased versions of the same tasks. Benchmarks such as BIG-bench embed a unique "canary" string in their files so model trainers can filter them out and evaluators can detect leaks.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading the visible score as the real score. If the grader's tests sit in the agent's workspace, assume the agent can read them, and possibly change them. A run where visible-test pass rate rises while hidden-test pass rate falls is the signature of gaming. Always report both, and treat a widening gap as a bug in the harness.

⚠️ Watch out

Treating a judge failure as a score. When json.loads throws, it's tempting to return 0. That silently penalizes answers the judge choked on, and if you return 5 on errors an agent can earn points by breaking the judge. Return None, count those cases, and send them to a person.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A task has n = 4 samples and c = 0 passes. What is pass@3?

  • With no passing samples, every draw of 3 comes from the failures, so C(4, 3) / C(4, 3) = 1 and pass@3 = 0.

  • That would treat each draw as a separate chance to pass, but none of the samples ever passed.

  • The estimator only needs n ≥ k, and 4 ≥ 3.

Show answer

A. With no passing samples, every draw of 3 comes from the failures, so C(4, 3) / C(4, 3) = 1 and pass@3 = 0.

2Agent B's visible-test pass rate went from 70% to 95%, and its hidden-test pass rate went from 60% to 55%. What's the most likely story?

  • Harder hidden tests would lower both runs equally, not move them in opposite directions.

  • A rising visible score with a falling hidden score is the classic sign of memorizing or tampering with visible tests.

  • Uncertainty matters, but opposite moves on two graders of the same tasks point to gaming, which you should investigate first.

Show answer

B. A rising visible score with a falling hidden score is the classic sign of memorizing or tampering with visible tests.

3Two agents ran the same 80 tasks. Why is a paired bootstrap on per-task differences better than comparing their two separate intervals?

  • Pairing doesn't change either score, only the uncertainty of the gap.

  • The number of resamples is your choice in both methods.

  • Easy tasks are easy for both agents. Resampling the differences keeps that pairing and gives a narrower, correct interval for the gap.

Show answer

C. Easy tasks are easy for both agents. Resampling the differences keeps that pairing and gives a narrower, correct interval for the gap.

Key takeaways

  • Pick the strictest grader the task allows: exact match for answers, hidden unit tests for code, a rubric judge only when nothing deterministic fits.
  • Keep tests the agent can see apart from tests that decide the score.
  • Compute pass@k per task with 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k), then average across tasks.
  • Every score gets a bootstrap interval and a task count; every comparison gets a paired interval.
  • Watch for gaming, overfitting to your dev set, and contamination, and keep a held-out set for the decisions that matter.

#Further reading

  • Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code (opens in a new tab): the Codex paper. Section 2.1 and Appendix A derive the unbiased pass@k estimator and give the stable NumPy version.
  • A statistical approach to model evaluations (opens in a new tab): Anthropic's five recommendations, including clustered standard errors and paired differences.
  • Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (opens in a new tab): the study that measured position, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias in model judges.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pin an evaluation task set by content hash so every report names the exact version it used.
  • Run agent-written code in a subprocess and grade it two ways: visible tests by exit code, and hidden tests by comparing outputs outside the sandbox.
  • Catch lookup-table answers and early-exit tricks, and count them as signals instead of hiding them.
  • Report pass@1, pass@3, tokens, and cost per solved task with bootstrap intervals and a paired comparison.

You'll build evalkit, a small evaluation runner, and use it to compare two agents. Both are scripted models with the harness's complete(messages, tools) interface, so everything runs offline and gives the same numbers every time. One agent, careful, writes real solutions and sometimes gets them wrong. The other, tuned, came out of weeks of prompt tweaking against the visible-test score, and it shows.

At the end, the naive grader will rank tuned first with a perfect score, and the strict grader will show it solving under a fifth of its attempts. Run the cells in order; each one uses names from the cells above it.

#Step 1: Pin the task set

Eight small coding tasks, each with two visible tests (shown to the agent) and three hidden ones (never shown). A test is a list whose last item is the expected result and whose other items are the arguments. The file gets a short SHA-256 fingerprint, which goes into every report: if someone edits a test, the version changes and old scores stop being comparable.

Look at the visible tests for median, slugify, and is_leap: none of them would catch the most common bug for that function. That's realistic. Prompt examples are chosen to explain the task, not to test it.

#Step 2: Script two agents

Both agents are ScriptedModels from harness/model.py, repeated in the cell below so this page runs on its own (in your project, import them instead). Each reply is one attempt at a task. A plan string per task says what each attempt will be: G for a correct solution, B for a plausible bug, L for a lookup table built from the visible examples, and X for code that exits the process early. Because a script doesn't read its prompt, the replies are listed in the order the runner will ask: all attempts at the first task, then the next.

The prompt is what a real model would see: the task, the function name, and the two visible examples. The usage numbers come from the same rough four-characters-per-token estimate as Module 1. They're consistent across both agents, which is all a comparison needs.

#Step 3: Grade the obvious way

The first grader is the one most people write first: put the code and the visible tests in a temporary directory, run them in a fresh python -I process with a timeout, and call it a pass if the process exits with code 0. That's also how Module 3's run_tests_in decides passed, which is fine for giving an agent feedback and, as you're about to see, not fine for scoring it. The run_python below is a cut-down stand-in for Module 3's sandbox runner: same call, same result keys, fewer limits.

Grading is deterministic, so both graders are wrapped in lru_cache: the same code for the same task is only run once. With scripted agents that repeat answers, this cuts the work by about two-thirds.

By this grader, tuned is perfect and careful misses almost a fifth. If you stopped here you'd ship the wrong agent.

#Step 4: Read what the winner wrote

Never trust a score you haven't looked behind. Print two of tuned's attempts at clamp:

The first attempt is a dictionary of the two inputs it was shown. The second never defines clamp at all: os._exit(0) ends the process with code 0 before a single assertion runs, and the naive grader reads that as success. Neither is far-fetched. Optimizing hard against tests a program can see or sidestep tends to find shortcuts like these, and surveys of reward hacking include coding models that went further and edited the unit tests themselves.

#Step 5: Keep the answers outside the sandbox

The strict grader changes three things.

  1. Hidden tests count. The score uses visible and hidden tests together.
  2. Expected answers never enter the sandbox. The runner receives only the inputs, prints the outputs, and the comparison happens in the grader's own process. Candidate code can read every file in its directory, so a tests.json full of answers is an answer key.
  3. Success has to be proven. The grader puts a random secret (a nonce) in a request file, and the runner deletes that file before any candidate code runs. Only a line that starts with the secret counts as a report. Exiting early produces no report, which the grader labels no-report instead of quietly failing it.

careful passes 27 of its 40 attempts. tuned drops to 7, and its three early exits show up as no-report. In a real harness, any no-report should page a human: a process that exits cleanly without finishing its tests is almost never an accident.

📝 Note

The nonce raises the bar but isn't a wall. The runner and the candidate share one process, so a determined program could dig the secret out of the runner's memory. Stronger designs run the candidate behind a narrow interface in its own process, or check results from outside the sandbox entirely. Hidden tests plus answers-stay-outside already stop the two exploits you saw.

#Step 6: Report pass@k, tokens, and cost

Now compute the numbers from the last lesson for both agents: pass@k per task and then averaged, tokens per attempt, and dollars per solved task, which is the number a budget owner actually cares about. The prices are made-up example rates, so only the comparison means anything.

Per attempt, the two agents cost about the same; tuned's lookup tables are a little longer than real solutions. Per solved task, tuned costs more than five times as much, because most of what it pays for doesn't work. A dashboard that tracks tokens per call would never show that. pass@3 is much higher than pass@1 for both agents, so sampling three attempts and keeping one that passes the hidden tests would be worth it here.

#Step 7: Error bars and a paired comparison

Eight tasks is a small eval, and the intervals should say so. Bootstrap each agent's per-task pass rate, then bootstrap the per-task difference on hidden tests, reusing the same resampled task indices for every series so the comparison stays paired.

Most intervals span 25 points or more, because eight tasks can't pin down a rate precisely. (tuned's visible score has no spread only because it passed every visible test on every task.) The paired gap is a different story: careful beats tuned on every single task, so every resample shows a positive gap, and 95% of them show at least 0.4. A small eval can still settle a large, consistent difference. It can't settle a three-point one.

#The finished runner

Here is the whole thing as one call, run on a fresh pair of agents. Every piece is defined in the steps above; evaluate wires them in order and returns one report row per agent. Thanks to the cache, this pass starts no new processes.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the strict runner receive only the test inputs and not the expected outputs?

  • The JSON is tiny either way; speed isn't the reason.

  • A candidate could open tests.json and return the expected value for each input. Comparing outside the sandbox removes that option.

  • They're plain lists, numbers, booleans, and None, all valid JSON.

Show answer

B. A candidate could open tests.json and return the expected value for each input. Comparing outside the sandbox removes that option.

2An agent's attempt gets the verdict no-report with return code 0. What should the harness do?

  • Exit code 0 is exactly what the early-exit trick fakes. The tests never reported.

  • Retrying hides the behavior you most need to know about.

  • Clean exits without a report almost always mean tampering or a broken runner, and both need a human.

Show answer

C. Clean exits without a report almost always mean tampering or a broken runner, and both need a human.

3careful and tuned use about the same number of tokens per attempt. Why is "$ per solve" the better cost metric for choosing between them?

  • Cheap attempts that fail still cost money. Dividing total cost by solved tasks reflects what you pay per useful result.

  • It includes both input and output tokens.

  • You could bootstrap any of them; that's not the reason to prefer it.

Show answer

A. Cheap attempts that fail still cost money. Dividing total cost by solved tasks reflects what you pay per useful result.

Key takeaways

  • Fingerprint the task file and print the version in every report.
  • The naive grader (visible tests, exit code) rewarded a lookup table and os._exit(0) with a perfect score.
  • Keep expected answers out of the sandbox, require a per-run secret in the report, and label clean exits without a report as no-report.
  • Report hidden pass@k, tokens, and cost per solved task together, each with an interval when it's a rate.
  • With few tasks, intervals are wide, but a paired comparison can still settle a large, consistent gap.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a third agent that sometimes writes while True: pass, and check that the timeout path reports timeout without stalling the run.
  • Track wall-clock time per attempt and add median latency to the report.
  • Write a diff_reports(old, new) function that refuses to compare reports whose task versions differ.
  • Replace the tuned agent's lookup tables with code that reads tests.json, then confirm the strict grader is unaffected because it never writes that file.

#Further reading

  • subprocess: Subprocess management (opens in a new tab): the official docs for run, timeout, and TimeoutExpired, which the sandboxed runner relies on.
  • SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? (opens in a new tab): a widely used coding-agent benchmark that grades patches with tests the model never sees.
  • Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning (opens in a new tab): Lilian Weng's survey of how optimized systems exploit their reward, including coding models that modify unit tests.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write graders that accept the right answers and only those.
  • Keep a held-out set stable and rarely used.
  • Stop a judge from being argued with, and measure how far to trust it.
  • Show by simulation why the unbiased pass@k estimator matters.
  • Flag likely contamination, and make ship decisions from paired intervals.

The cells on this page share variables, like a notebook. Run the warm-up first, since later solutions use its pass_at_k.

#Warm-up: predict pass@k

A task was attempted 4 times and passed once. Before you run the cell, write down pass@1, pass@2, and pass@4.

pass@1 is the plain pass rate, 1/4. For pass@2, 3 of the 6 possible pairs avoid the one passing attempt, so the answer is 1 − 3/6. Drawing all 4 attempts is certain to include the pass.

#Exercise 1: Grade numeric answers with a tolerance

Agents write numbers inside sentences: "x = 3.333", "the total is 1,250.0". Write grade_numeric(output, expected, rel_tol=1e-3) that takes the last number in the output (commas allowed) and compares it to expected with a relative tolerance. "About 3.3" should fail for 10/3, since it's off by 1%.

Need a hint?

re.findall(r"-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?", text) finds the numbers. Strip commas first. math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=...) handles the tolerance.

Show solution

Taking the last number skips intermediate working like "Step 2 gives 7". A relative tolerance scales with the answer, so 1e-3 means "within 0.1%" whether the answer is 3 or 3 million.

#Exercise 2: A held-out split that never reshuffles

random.shuffle with a seed gives a different split as soon as you add tasks, so tasks quietly move from held-out into dev, where you've been tuning on them. Write split_of(task_id) that hashes the id with SHA-256 and puts about 20% of tasks in held-out. Show that adding 20 tasks moves none of the original 40. Then wrap the held-out tasks in a class that refuses a fourth evaluation.

Need a hint?

int(hashlib.sha256(task_id.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100 gives a stable bucket from 0 to 99 that depends only on the id.

Show solution

A task's bucket depends only on its own id, so new tasks can't push old ones across the line. The run budget is a speed bump for people: each look at held-out scores leaks a little information into your next decision.

#Exercise 3: A tripwire for judge injection

Agents being graded by a model judge can write text aimed at the judge. Write grader_injection(answer) that returns the regex patterns an answer matches, and safe_judge(judge, task, answer) that sends flagged answers to a person instead of the judge. Catch at least: "ignore the rubric/instructions", a score stated in the answer, "note to the grader", a line starting with SYSTEM:, and a fake </answer> tag.

Need a hint?

Use re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE so ^ matches at the start of every line. Call the judge only when the pattern list comes back empty.

Show solution

This is a tripwire, not a wall: a paraphrased attack will slip past any regex list. Its value is cheap detection of lazy attempts and a count you can track over time. The real defenses are delimiting the answer, a strict output format, and deterministic checks for anything that can be checked.

#Exercise 4: How much should you trust the judge?

People labeled 12 answers pass or fail; the judge labeled the same 12. Compute raw agreement and Cohen's kappa, which subtracts the agreement two raters would reach by chance: kappa = (agreement − chance) / (1 − chance). Then look at the answer lengths where they disagree.

Need a hint?

Chance agreement is P(both say pass) + P(both say fail) if they labeled independently: p_h * p_j + (1 - p_h) * (1 - p_j), where p_h and p_j are each rater's pass rates.

Show solution

Two-thirds agreement sounds fine until you see that coin-flip raters would reach one half. Kappa of 0.33 is weak. The disagreements have a pattern: every bad answer the judge passed was long, which is verbosity bias. Fix the rubric (for example, "length earns no credit") and measure again before using this judge.

#Exercise 5: Prove the shortcut pass@k is biased

Simulate a task whose true pass rate is 0.2. Draw n = 10 attempts 20,000 times. For each draw, compute the unbiased estimator and the plug-in formula 1 − (1 − c/n)^5, then compare both averages with the true pass@5 = 1 − 0.8^5.

Need a hint?

np.random.default_rng(1).binomial(10, 0.2, size=20_000) gives 20,000 values of c at once.

Show solution

The plug-in version underestimates by about 8 points, every time, no matter how many tasks you average. Since (1 − p)^k curves upward, plugging in a noisy estimate of p overshoots it on average, which pulls pass@k down. Averaging more tasks shrinks noise, but not bias.

#Exercise 6: Spot likely contamination

You re-ran six public tasks with freshly written paraphrases that test the same skill. Flag tasks whose pass rate drops by 0.5 or more. For one flagged task, measure how much of the published reference solution's 5-token sequences appear in the agent's output (containment), and compare with an independent solution.

Need a hint?

Tokenize with re.findall(r"\w+|[^\w\s]", text), build a set of 5-token tuples for each text, and divide the shared count by the reference's count.

Show solution

A big drop on paraphrases plus a near-verbatim copy of the published solution, variable names included, points to memorization rather than skill. Neither signal proves contamination alone: paraphrases can accidentally be harder, and short standard algorithms look alike. Together they're a strong reason to replace those tasks.

#Exercise 7: Ship, or keep measuring?

Agents A and B ran 30 tasks, 3 attempts each. Write decide(a, b) that bootstraps the per-task difference and returns "B is better", "A is better", or "no decision" depending on whether the 95% interval excludes zero. Then, as a thought experiment, tile both arrays three times to see what 90 tasks with the same pattern would show.

Need a hint?

Draw one index matrix and apply it to b - a, so both agents are always resampled on the same tasks.

Show solution

Same gap, narrower interval. Tripling the tasks shrinks the interval by about √3, which is the whole case for writing more tasks before arguing about a five-point difference. Tiling is only a thought experiment: copies of the same tasks aren't new evidence, so in practice you'd write 60 new ones.

#Challenge: Catch an agent that edits the tests

Before an agent runs, record a manifest of SHA-256 hashes for every file in its workspace. Afterward, report any test file that was added, modified, or deleted, including conftest.py and pytest.ini, which can change what pytest collects. Simulate an agent that guts one test, deletes another, and adds a conftest.py that ignores the tests folder.

Need a hint?

os.walk visits every file. Compare the two manifests' key sets for adds and deletes, and their values for edits.

Show solution

The agent never touched app.py, and add still subtracts. Without the manifest, a test run after this "fix" would report success. The surest version of this check is simpler still: copy the tests in from a trusted location right before grading, so nothing the agent did to them matters. The .replace(os.sep, "/") keeps the prefix check working on Windows, where paths use backslashes.

What you'll learn

  • Route requests with cheap rules first, a model classifier second, and a person when neither is sure.
  • Describe the planner, worker, and reviewer roles and what each one is allowed to see and do.
  • Write handoffs as structured messages that a receiver can validate before acting.
  • Choose between shared state and message passing, and prevent lost updates when agents share state.
  • Estimate whether a multi-agent design will cost more or less than one agent.

Imagine a team that splits one coding agent into five, and reads this in the first run's log. The planner asked two workers to "improve error handling". One wrapped every call in try/except and returned None. The other made every function raise a custom exception. Both passed their own tests, the merge broke 14 others, and the run used about four times the tokens of the single agent it replaced.

Nothing in that story is a model failure. Each agent did a reasonable thing with what it was told. The failure was in the system around them: a vague handoff, overlapping work, no shared definition of done, and no check before merging. Multi-agent design is mostly about those seams.

#Routers: pick the right agent, or admit you can't

A router looks at a request and sends it to one specialized agent: a code agent with write access, a docs agent, a triage agent that only reads logs. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" lists routing as one of its basic workflow patterns. The design question is what happens when the router is wrong or unsure.

Rules go first because they're free, fast, and predictable. The classifier handles the rest, and its answer is accepted only if the route exists and the confidence clears a threshold you tuned on labeled requests.

Look at the last line. The classifier was 99% confident in a route called deploy, which doesn't exist. A router that trusted the label would have crashed or, worse, matched it to something close. Confidence is the model's opinion; the list of routes is your policy. Check both.

#Planner, workers, reviewer

For tasks that need several steps, the common shape is the one Anthropic calls orchestrator-workers, plus a review loop. A planner breaks the request into subtasks with clear outputs. Workers each do one subtask with only the context and tools that subtask needs. A reviewer checks the combined result against acceptance criteria and either approves it or sends specific feedback back to one worker, a bounded number of times.

Two rules make this work. Give each subtask an owner for every file it may touch, so two workers never edit the same thing (that's the opening story's bug). And make the reviewer independent: it didn't write the code, it runs the tests itself rather than trusting a worker's "tests pass", and it has read access only. A reviewer that can edit will "fix" things instead of reporting them, and then nobody reviews the reviewer.

#Handoffs are contracts, not chat

When one agent passes work to another, free text like "fix the date thing" loses everything the sender knew. A handoff should be a structured message that the receiver (or the orchestrator) can validate before any tokens are spent.

The good handoff names the file, the function, the failing test, and three ways to tell when the job is done. The trace_id ties every message in a run together, so the traces from Module 4 can show the whole conversation across agents. The vague one fails four checks before a worker wastes a single call on it.

#Shared state or message passing?

Agents can coordinate in two ways. With shared state (often called a blackboard), every agent reads and writes one common store. With message passing, agents only see what's sent to them, and one orchestrator applies results. Shared state is convenient, and it's where lost updates come from:

Without a version check, B's write silently erased A's timeout. With one (a compare-and-set), B's stale write is rejected, B re-reads, and both changes survive.

Message passing has a security benefit too: each agent sees only what it's sent. On a shared board, a prompt injection that one agent reads from a web page can steer every agent that reads the board afterward. The tradeoff is the one Cognition's "Don't Build Multi-Agents" essay argues: agents that see too little make conflicting decisions. A good compromise is a single writer (the orchestrator), read-only shared context where it's needed, and handoffs that carry the decisions already made.

#When splitting helps, and when it only costs

Every model call re-sends its whole context, and contexts grow as an agent works, so input tokens grow roughly with the square of the number of steps. That one fact explains both sides of the argument:

When subtasks are truly independent and need small briefings, splitting is cheaper and faster, because workers run in parallel with short contexts. When every worker has to re-read the whole codebase to do its piece, the same split costs about 30% more than one agent. In practice teams also give multi-agent systems more work, not the same work: Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system used about 15 times as many tokens as a chat, worth it for broad research questions but not for most coding tasks, which have fewer parallel pieces.

Reach for multiple agents when the work is parallel (many independent searches), when roles need different permissions (a reviewer that can't write), or when you want independent verification. Stay with one agent when the steps are tightly coupled, when every step needs the full context, or when the task is small enough that coordination is most of the cost.

⚠️ Watch out

Forwarding the whole transcript. Giving each worker the planner's entire conversation "for context" feels safe, but it multiplies token cost and hands every worker every earlier mistake and every injected instruction. Send the handoff's fields and the files it names, and let workers ask for more through a tool.

⚠️ Watch out

A review loop with no exit. A reviewer that keeps finding something to change and a worker that keeps changing it will run until the budget dies. Cap revisions (two is common), require the reviewer's feedback to cite a failing acceptance check, and send the third failure to a person.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A classifier returns {"route": "billing", "confidence": 0.97}, but your routes are code, docs, and triage. What should the router do?

  • Guessing a route the model didn't pick hides the error and sends work to an agent with the wrong tools.

  • High confidence doesn't make an unknown route valid. The list of routes is your policy; a person can decide or add a route.

  • The threshold only applies to known routes.

Show answer

B. High confidence doesn't make an unknown route valid. The list of routes is your policy; a person can decide or add a route.

2Two workers update the same shared config. Worker B's write is rejected by a version check. What's the right next step for B?

  • That overwrites A's change, which is the lost update the check exists to stop.

  • This is compare-and-set: B merges its change onto the latest state, so neither update is lost.

  • Occasional conflicts are normal with shared state; retrying on the latest version handles them.

Show answer

B. This is compare-and-set: B merges its change onto the latest state, so neither update is lost.

3Which task benefits most from splitting into a planner and several workers?

  • Every edit depends on the same decision, so splitting invites conflicting edits.

  • Each package check is independent and needs a small briefing, so workers can run in parallel with short contexts.

  • The coordination would cost more than the whole task.

Show answer

B. Each package check is independent and needs a small briefing, so workers can run in parallel with short contexts.

Key takeaways

  • Route with rules first, a classifier second, and a human queue when the route is unknown or the model is unsure.
  • Planners split work, workers own disjoint pieces, and an independent read-only reviewer checks results against acceptance criteria with a revision cap.
  • Handoffs are validated structured messages with a task, inputs, acceptance criteria, a budget, and a trace id.
  • Shared state needs version checks; message passing with a single writer avoids lost updates and limits how far an injection spreads.
  • Splitting helps when work is parallel and briefings are small; it costs more when every agent needs the full context.

#Further reading

  • Building effective agents (opens in a new tab): Anthropic's catalog of workflow patterns (routing, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) and its case for starting simple.
  • How we built our multi-agent research system (opens in a new tab): a detailed account of a lead agent with parallel subagents, including the token costs and the tasks it suits poorly.
  • Don't Build Multi-Agents (opens in a new tab): the opposing view, with the principle that actions carry implicit decisions and conflicting decisions carry bad results.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Validate a planner's JSON plan for unknown workers, missing checks, overlapping file ownership, and attempts to edit tests.
  • Brief each worker with only its task, its files, and its acceptance checks.
  • Apply worker results through a single writer that drops edits outside a subtask's files.
  • Review with deterministic tests first and a model reviewer last, with a cap on revisions.
  • Account for tokens per agent so you can see what the split cost.

You'll build the pipeline from the last lesson's second diagram and run it on a tiny shop codebase with two failing tests and a README to update. Every agent is a ScriptedModel, so the run is offline and identical each time, but the pipeline code doesn't know that: it would drive real models the same way.

By the end, the run log will show a worker's buggy first attempt being sent back with the exact failing assertion, a docs worker's out-of-scope edit being dropped, and a final test gate before the reviewer is asked anything.

#Step 1: The codebase and the model interface

The first cell repeats the scripted model from harness/model.py so this page runs by itself, then sets up four files. test_shop.py was written by a person and describes what "done" means; no agent is allowed to edit it.

#Step 2: Script the team

Each agent replies with JSON. The planner returns a plan in which every subtask names a worker, the files it owns, and acceptance checks that a program can verify: a test that must pass, or text a file must contain. The code worker's second reply is a deliberate bug, and the docs worker oversteps by "tidying" a file it doesn't own. Those are the two failures the pipeline has to handle.

make_team builds fresh agents each time, because a scripted model's replies are used up as it's called. The script order matches the order the pipeline will ask: all three subtasks first, then the one revision.

#Step 3: Get a plan and validate it

The planner's output is a proposal, not a command. Before any worker runs, check it against your policy: every worker exists, every subtask has checks, no two subtasks own the same file, and nobody owns a test.

The real plan passes. The bad one fails four ways, and each failure would have caused a real problem: work routed to an agent that doesn't exist, a subtask nobody can declare finished, two workers editing pricing.py, and a worker allowed to rewrite the tests it's graded by.

#Step 4: Brief each worker with only what it needs

A briefing has the subtask, the files that subtask owns, the acceptance checks, and (on a retry) the reviewer's feedback. It doesn't include the planner's conversation, the other subtasks, or files the worker can't change.

Here the whole repository is only about 200 tokens, so the savings look small. In a real project the repository might be 200,000 tokens while each briefing stays near 100, and every token a worker doesn't see is also an instruction it can't be misled by.

#Step 5: Apply results through one writer

Workers don't write files. They return results, and the orchestrator applies them. That makes the orchestrator the single writer from the last lesson, so it can enforce ownership in one place.

The README change is applied and the edit to inventory.py is dropped, while the subtask itself continues. Dropping is gentler than failing the whole subtask, but it should never be silent: the pipeline logs every rejected path, and a worker that keeps reaching outside its files is a signal worth alerting on.

#Step 6: Review with tests first

The reviewer's first job is mechanical. Write the files to a temporary directory, run python -I -m unittest -v in a subprocess, and read each test's status from the output. It's Module 3's run_tests_in idea with one change: the verbose output gives a status per test, so failures can be traced to the subtask that owns them. Then map tests back to subtasks through their acceptance checks. Here are the tests before any agent has touched the code:

reasons holds the one line from each failure that a worker can act on, such as '$10.5' != '$10.50'. That line becomes the feedback in the worker's next briefing. A reviewer note that just says "tests fail" gives the worker nothing to fix.

#The finished pipeline

run_pipeline puts the steps in order. Subtasks that pass their checks leave the pending dictionary; failed ones get their failures as feedback, up to MAX_REVISIONS extra attempts, and then a person. After the loop, a final gate re-runs every test, because a fix to one subtask can break another. Only then does the model reviewer see the diff, and its job is the part tests can't judge: whether the change stayed in scope and the docs match the code.

Read the log from the top. t2's first attempt used round(), which turns 10.50 into 10.5; the test caught it, the feedback quoted the assertion, and the second attempt switched to integer math. t3's stray edit was rejected without derailing the subtask. The token line shows where the money went: the code worker made three calls, and the reviewer's single call was large because it read every changed file. With real models and a larger codebase, that table is what tells you whether the split paid for itself.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why do the deterministic tests run before the model reviewer is called?

  • Asking a model to judge code that fails its tests wastes a call, and the model might approve it anyway.

  • It can; it reads every changed file. The order is about cost and trust, not ability.

  • The tests run without any model involved.

Show answer

A. Asking a model to judge code that fails its tests wastes a call, and the model might approve it anyway.

2After t2's revision passes test_format_price, why does the pipeline re-run all the tests instead of finishing?

  • The final gate is there for real models too; determinism isn't the concern.

  • t1 passed earlier, but t2's files could affect it. Only a full run at the end shows the combined result works.

  • -v reports every test's status.

Show answer

B. t1 passed earlier, but t2's files could affect it. Only a full run at the end shows the combined result works.

3The docs worker returned edits to README.md and inventory.py, but owns only README.md. What did the orchestrator do, and why?

  • Notes aren't permission. Ownership comes from the validated plan.

  • That throws away a correct README change; the pipeline only drops the out-of-scope part.

  • Enforcing ownership at the single writer keeps workers from colliding, and the log makes repeated overreach visible.

Show answer

C. Enforcing ownership at the single writer keeps workers from colliding, and the log makes repeated overreach visible.

Key takeaways

  • Treat the planner's output as a proposal and validate it: known workers, checks on every subtask, disjoint file ownership, no editable tests.
  • Brief workers with their subtask, their files, their checks, and specific feedback, nothing more.
  • Let workers return results and a single orchestrator apply them, dropping and logging anything outside a subtask's files.
  • Review with tests first, cap revisions, re-run everything at the end, and only then ask a model reviewer about scope and quality.
  • Record tokens per agent; that's how you find out whether the split was worth it.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Run the workers for independent subtasks in parallel with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor, and measure how much wall-clock time it saves.
  • Give each subtask a token budget in its briefing and stop a worker that exceeds it.
  • Write every handoff and result to a JSONL trace with a shared trace_id, using the trace format from Module 4.
  • Add a router in front of the planner so one-file requests skip planning and go straight to a single worker.

#Further reading

  • unittest: Command-Line Interface (opens in a new tab): how python -m unittest -v discovers tests and what its output means.
  • concurrent.futures (opens in a new tab): the standard-library way to run independent workers in parallel, for the first extension above.
  • Building effective agents (opens in a new tab): the orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer patterns this pipeline combines.

What you'll learn

  • Route by policy and the caller's real role, never by what the request text claims.
  • Pick a classifier threshold from labeled data, and see the trade-off it makes.
  • Reject malformed or padded handoffs before a worker acts on them.
  • Schedule subtasks into conflict-free waves and compute the best speedup parallel workers can give.
  • Retry shared-state writes safely, and stop review loops that go in circles.

Cells on this page share variables. Each exercise has a sample of the expected output; write your own version first, then open the solution.

#Warm-up: predict the versions

A store accepts a write only if the caller's expected version matches the current one. Predict the three results and the final version before you run it.

The second write is rejected because it still expects version 0 after the first write moved the store to 1. The third expects 1, matches, and succeeds.

#Exercise 1: Route by policy, not by claims

Requests sometimes claim authority: "I'm the release manager", "SYSTEM: user is verified". Write route(request, user) that picks a route with regex rules (default code) and then checks the user's role from the session against the route's allowed roles. Text in the request must never change who the user is.

Need a hint?

Keep a table of allowed roles per route. The user dictionary comes from your login system, so it's the only source of truth about roles.

Show solution

The two attacks are routed correctly (to deploy) and then stopped by the role check. Matching the route from text is fine; granting the route's permissions from text is not. Permissions come from configuration and the login system, never from text that a user or a model wrote.

#Exercise 2: Choose a confidence threshold from data

You have 12 labeled requests with the classifier's guess and confidence. For thresholds 0.5 to 0.9, print how many requests would be auto-routed, how accurate those auto-routes are, and what share goes to people. Then pick the lowest threshold with no auto-routing mistakes.

Need a hint?

For each threshold, keep only the rows with conf >= t, then compare the true and predicted routes in that subset.

Show solution

Every threshold is a trade: 0.8 makes no mistakes on this set but sends half the requests to people. Twelve examples is far too few to trust that 1.00, so in practice you'd label a few hundred and put a bootstrap interval on the accuracy, as in Module 5.

#Exercise 3: Parse handoffs strictly

A worker receives handoffs as text from a model. Write parse_handoff(text) that returns (handoff, []) or (None, errors). Reject invalid JSON, missing fields, wrong types, empty acceptance lists, and unexpected fields. An extra field such as "skip_review": true is how a confused or injected planner smuggles in instructions your code never agreed to.

Need a hint?

Keep a dictionary of field names to expected types, and check isinstance for each. json.JSONDecodeError has a short .msg.

Show solution

Rejecting unknown fields is the important line. Lenient parsing ("ignore what you don't recognize") is a fine default for public web APIs, but between agents an unrecognized field is either a bug or an attack, and both deserve a loud error.

#Exercise 4: Schedule subtasks so no two edit the same file

Six subtasks touch overlapping files. Write waves(subtasks) that groups them into waves: subtasks in one wave share no files and can run in parallel, and each wave runs after the previous one. Use a greedy pass in plan order.

Need a hint?

For each wave, keep a set of files already claimed. Take a subtask if its files don't intersect that set, and remove it from the remaining list.

Show solution

Greedy isn't always optimal (finding the fewest waves is graph coloring, which is hard in general), but it's predictable and good enough for plans with a handful of subtasks. If a plan needs many waves, that's a hint the work is too coupled to split.

#Exercise 5: Compare-and-set with retries

Write update(board, change, max_retries=3) that reads the board, applies change to a copy, and writes with the version it read. On a conflict, it re-reads and tries again, giving up after max_retries. Test it against a rival agent that sneaks in a write during your first two attempts.

Need a hint?

Apply the change to freshly read data on every attempt. Retrying with stale data would just overwrite the rival again.

Show solution

Both rival writes survive, and so does timeout. The retry cap matters: under heavy contention, unbounded retries become a loop of their own, and Module 7 is about stopping those.

#Exercise 6: How much can parallel workers save?

Each subtask has a duration and a list of subtasks it depends on. One agent working alone takes the sum of all durations. With unlimited parallel workers, the run still can't finish faster than the critical path, the longest chain of dependencies. Compute both, the path itself, and the best possible speedup.

Need a hint?

A task can start when its slowest dependency finishes: finish[t] = duration[t] + max(finish[d] for d in deps). Memoize with a dictionary, and remember which dependency was the slowest so you can walk the path backward.

Show solution

Even with infinite workers, this plan gets at most 1.66 times faster, while paying for a coordinator and a briefing per worker. Speeding up anything off the critical path (like auth) changes nothing. If you want a faster run, shorten db or tests, or split them.

#Challenge: Stop reviewer ping-pong

A worker and a reviewer can loop forever: the reviewer asks for spaces around *, the next reviewer pass asks for them removed, and the files flip back and forth. Write review_loop(worker_versions, reviewer_ok, max_rounds=6) that hashes the files after each round and stops as soon as a state repeats, before the round cap.

Need a hint?

json.dumps(files, sort_keys=True) gives a stable string to hash. Keep a dictionary from hash to the round that first produced it.

Show solution

A repeated state means the loop can't make progress, however many rounds are left, so stopping early saves the remaining budget. The same check catches agents that delegate a task back and forth, which is where Module 7 picks up.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Share one budget for steps, tokens, dollars, and time across a team, with a slice per agent, checked before each call.
  • Detect delegation cycles, rounds without progress, and agents that keep editing after the checks pass.
  • Require human approval for irreversible actions, bound to the exact action, single use, and expiring.
  • Give each agent a credential with only the scopes its role needs, kept out of the model's context.
  • Keep a tamper-evident audit log, and gate releases on a written checklist with a rollback plan.

Picture the log of an overnight run. At 2:14 a.m. every test passed. The team kept going anyway: the reviewer asked for a refactor, the worker made it, a test broke, and the planner handed the fix back to the worker, over and over. By 7 a.m. there were 1,900 model calls, 62 commits on the branch, and one force-push to main, which the worker's token allowed and nobody had approved.

Every agent behaved reasonably one step at a time. What was missing was the harness around them: a budget for the whole run, a rule for "done", a check that rounds were making progress, an approval step before an irreversible push, and a token too narrow to push to main at all. Module 2 gave one agent a step limit, a stuck rule for repeated calls, and a token budget. This lesson scales those ideas up to a team and to actions in the real world.

#One budget for the whole team

Separate per-agent limits don't add up to a run limit. Five agents with 50 steps each can still make 250 calls, and a planner that spawns workers can multiply that further. So the budget belongs to the run, and each agent draws from a slice of what's left. The budget covers four things, because each fails differently: steps (runaway loops), tokens (huge contexts), dollars (expensive models), and wall-clock time (calls that hang).

Check the budget before a call, using an estimate of its size. Checking after, as Module 2's BudgetModel did, lets the last call push you over.

The worker hit its own slice first: call 6 would have taken it to 17,400 tokens against a 15,000 limit, so the call never happened. Every reservation was also charged to the parent run, so run.used shows the true total. time.monotonic() is used for the deadline because, unlike the wall clock, it never jumps when the computer's clock is adjusted.

#Loops that exact-repeat checks miss

Module 2's is_stuck catches one agent calling the same tool with the same arguments again and again. Teams loop in ways that look like work:

  • Delegation cycles. A task passes from planner to coder to tester and back to coder, and nobody does it.
  • No progress. Every round makes a different edit, but the same tests keep failing.
  • Not stopping when done. The checks pass, and the team keeps "improving" things, which is how the overnight run broke a passing build.

A delegation cycle is easy to see if you track the chain of agents a task has passed through. Step through it:

Revisions are different: a reviewer sending work back with a specific failure is fine, and Module 6 capped those. A cycle is the same task bouncing without anyone doing it.

The other two need a measure of progress. Here it's the set of failing tests: a round counts as progress only if fewer tests fail than ever before. The monitor also remembers every state it has seen, and declares "done" the moment nothing fails, so the harness can stop accepting edits.

Round 4 fixed nothing and broke test_c; round 5 undid that, which is still no better than round 2. Three rounds without a new best is the stop. Measuring progress by your own checks, not by the agents' reports, is what makes this work: agents are very good at describing activity as progress.

#Approvals for actions you can't take back

Sort every tool into tiers. Reading files and running tests in the sandbox happen automatically. Writes inside the agent's own branch or workspace also happen automatically, because they're logged and easy to undo. Anything that leaves the sandbox or can't be undone (pushing to a shared branch, deleting, sending a message, spending money, changing permissions) waits for a person. Anything not on the list is denied.

An approval must be bound to the exact action, not to a tool. "Yes, push" for fix/dates must not also allow a push to main. So the approval is stored under a hash of the tool and its arguments, used once, and expires.

The push to main is refused because the approval was for a different branch. The second push to fix/dates is refused because the approval was used up. And drop_database isn't on the list at all, so it's denied without asking anyone, which is the right default for tools you didn't plan for.

Approval doesn't replace a way back. Before any approved change, record how to undo it: the commit to revert, the backup to restore. A person approving a push is betting the change is good; rollback is what you do when the bet loses.

#Least privilege: one narrow credential per agent

The overnight force-push happened because the worker held a token that could push to main. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications names this risk excessive agency and traces it to three causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy. The fix for permissions is a separate credential per agent, scoped to its role, expiring soon, and never placed in the model's context. Tools look the token up; the model only sees tool names.

Even if a prompt injection convinced the reviewer to push code, its token can't write. Even if the worker were told to merge, it lacks main:merge. And a token stolen from a log is useless an hour later. The same idea exists in real tools: GitHub's fine-grained personal access tokens are limited to chosen repositories and permissions with an expiration date, and a GitHub Actions workflow can shrink its automatic token like this:

#An audit log that can't be quietly edited

Module 4's traces are for debugging. An audit log answers a different question: who did what, and who allowed it. That makes it a target, since the record of a bad push is exactly what an attacker or a misbehaving agent would want to change. A hash chain makes edits detectable: each entry stores the hash of the previous one, so changing any entry breaks every hash after it.

Editing entry 2 to turn a denial into an approval is caught immediately. The chain has a limit: someone who can rewrite the whole file can recompute every hash. So store the latest hash somewhere agents can't write, such as a separate service or a signed commit, and check against it.

#A release checklist

Nothing an agent team makes should reach main without passing a written gate. A good one is short enough to run every time:

  1. All tests pass from a clean checkout, not the agent's workspace.
  2. The hidden eval doesn't regress: the paired interval from Module 5 doesn't fall below zero.
  3. The diff touches only paths the plan allowed, and no test files.
  4. A secret scan of the diff finds nothing.
  5. Every risky action has a matching approval in the audit log, and the chain verifies.
  6. The run stayed within its budget.
  7. The rollback plan is written down: the commit to revert, or the tag to redeploy.

On GitHub, branch protection rules can enforce parts of this mechanically, such as requiring a pull request, passing status checks, and an approving review before a merge.

⚠️ Watch out

Putting the budget or the rules in the prompt. "You have 20 steps" and "never push to main" are requests, and a confused or injected model can ignore them. Limits and permissions have to live in the harness code and the credentials, where the model can't argue with them.

⚠️ Watch out

Approving a tool instead of an action. A button that says "allow git_push for this session" turns one approval into unlimited pushes to any branch. Bind each approval to a hash of the tool and its exact arguments, make it single use, and give it an expiry.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A person approved git_push with {"branch": "fix/dates"}. The agent then calls git_push with {"branch": "main"}. What does the gate do?

  • That treats the approval as covering the tool. The gate binds approvals to the exact arguments.

  • The approval is stored under a hash of the tool and its arguments, and main produces a different hash.

  • It would also fail if expired, but the first reason is that it's a different action.

Show answer

B. The approval is stored under a hash of the tool and its arguments, and main produces a different hash.

2A run's failing tests go: [a, b], [b], [b], [b, c], [b]. Why does the progress monitor stop at round 5 even though every round changed the code?

  • The best was one failing test in round 2. Rounds 3, 4, and 5 never did better, and patience was 3.

  • The files differ each round; the stop is about results, not files.

  • A new failure isn't a stop rule by itself; it's one more round without progress.

Show answer

A. The best was one failing test in round 2. Rounds 3, 4, and 5 never did better, and patience was 3.

3Why give the reviewer agent a token without branch:write, if its prompt already says not to edit code?

  • Cost has nothing to do with it.

  • Least privilege holds even when the model is confused or attacked. The prompt is a request; the credential is a limit.

  • The reviewer does need repo:read; it just doesn't need to write.

Show answer

B. Least privilege holds even when the model is confused or attacked. The prompt is a request; the credential is a limit.

Key takeaways

  • One budget per run (steps, tokens, dollars, time), sliced per agent and checked before each call.
  • Watch for delegation cycles, rounds without progress on your own checks, and teams that keep editing after everything passes.
  • Approvals are for irreversible actions, bound to the exact action, single use, and expiring, with a rollback plan recorded first.
  • Each agent gets its own short-lived credential with only its role's scopes, held by tools and never shown to the model.
  • A hash-chained audit log makes edits detectable, and a short release checklist decides what reaches main.

#Further reading

  • LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency (opens in a new tab): OWASP's description of the risk, its three causes, and mitigations, including requiring user approval.
  • Controlling permissions for GITHUB_TOKEN (opens in a new tab): how to narrow the token a GitHub Actions job gets.
  • About protected branches (opens in a new tab): the branch rules that can require reviews and passing checks before a merge.
